questions.sub_topic: Using heats of hydrogenation of butene isomers to compare alkene stability through hyperconjugation and steric strain, and X-ray evidence for resonance in carbonate
questions.question: Enthalpies of hydrogenation (kJ mol⁻¹) to butane are: but-1-ene −127, cis-but-2-ene −120 and trans-but-2-ene −116. X-ray studies also show that the three C–O bonds in the carbonate ion are of equal length, intermediate between C–O and C=O. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) But-1-ene is the most stable isomer because it releases the most heat on hydrogenation; the carbonate ion has one double and two single bonds that rapidly exchange places
B) All three alkenes are equally stable since all give butane; the equal C–O lengths mean carbonate has three double bonds
C) cis-But-2-ene is more stable than the trans isomer because the methyl groups attract each other; carbonate bond lengths are equal because carbon is sp³ hybridised

D) A smaller enthalpy of hydrogenation means a more stable alkene, so stability is trans-but-2-ene > cis-but-2-ene > but-1-ene; the but-2-enes have six α-hydrogens available for hyperconjugation (delocalisation of σ C–H electrons into the π system) against two in but-1-ene, and the trans isomer avoids the steric repulsion between the two methyl groups present in the cis isomer; the equal C–O bonds in carbonate show that it is a resonance hybrid of three equivalent canonical structures, with the charge delocalised
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) trans > cis > but-1-ene in stability; hyperconjugation and steric effects explain it; carbonate is a resonance hybrid.
Concept: Hyperconjugation is a general stabilising interaction involving delocalisation of σ electrons of a C–H bond of an alkyl group directly attached to an unsaturated system (or an atom with an unshared p orbital); the greater the number of α-hydrogens, the greater the stabilisation. Resonance: when a molecule cannot be represented by a single structure, its actual structure is a hybrid of canonical structures; the hybrid has lower energy than any canonical form and, for carbonate, equal bond lengths.
Why: All three isomers give the same product, so differences in the heat released reflect differences in the starting energies: less heat released means the alkene was lower in energy. Each extra α-hydrogen allows more hyperconjugation, stabilising the more substituted double bond, and in the cis isomer the two methyl groups on the same side crowd each other. In carbonate, the π electrons and negative charge are spread equally over the three oxygen atoms.
Why not the others: (A) More heat released means less stable; resonance structures are not real structures that interconvert. (B) Different heats show different stabilities, and carbonate has bonds of order about 1⅓. (C) The cis isomer suffers steric strain, and carbonate carbon is sp² hybridised.
Key point: Lower heat of hydrogenation = more stable alkene; more α-H (hyperconjugation) and trans geometry stabilise.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Products and gas mole ratios in the Kolbe electrolysis of sodium propanoate, and the oxygen needed to burn the alkane formed
questions.question: An aqueous solution of sodium propanoate is electrolysed (Kolbe's method). Which alkane is formed, what is the mole ratio of the gases produced at the anode and cathode, and how many moles of O₂ are needed for complete combustion of 1 mol of the alkane?
options: A) Propane; anode CO₂ only; cathode O₂; 5 mol O₂
B) Butane at the anode together with CO₂ in the ratio butane : CO₂ = 1 : 2, and H₂ at the cathode (1 mol per mol of butane), the solution becoming alkaline; burning 1 mol of butane needs 6.5 mol O₂
C) Ethane at the anode and CO₂ at the cathode; 3.5 mol O₂
D) Butane at the cathode and H₂ at the anode; 13 mol O₂
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Butane + 2CO₂ at the anode, H₂ at the cathode; 6.5 mol O₂ per mol of butane.
Concept: In Kolbe's electrolytic method, an aqueous solution of the sodium or potassium salt of a carboxylic acid is electrolysed, and an alkane containing an even number of carbon atoms is formed at the anode, by coupling of two alkyl radicals after loss of CO₂. Methane cannot be prepared by this method. Alkanes burn in excess air or oxygen to give CO₂ and water with the evolution of a large amount of heat; on heating to a higher temperature in the absence of air (pyrolysis or cracking), they break into lower alkanes, alkenes and hydrogen.
Given: salt CH₃CH₂COONa; electrolysis.
Formula/Principle: Anode: 2CH₃CH₂COO⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ + 2CO₂ + 2e⁻; cathode: 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻.
Step 1: Two ethyl radicals join: the alkane is butane, C₄H₁₀.
Step 2: Per 2 electrons: 1 mol butane + 2 mol CO₂ at the anode; 1 mol H₂ at the cathode, and OH⁻ makes the solution alkaline.
Step 3: C₄H₁₀ + (13/2)O₂ → 4CO₂ + 5H₂O ⇒ 6.5 mol O₂ per mol.
Why: Each carboxylate loses one electron at the anode, releases CO₂, and leaves an ethyl radical; two such radicals pair up. Water is reduced at the cathode because Na⁺ is much harder to reduce.
Why not the others: (A) The radicals pair, doubling the chain. (C) Ethane comes from acetate, and CO₂ is formed at the anode. (D) The electrodes are swapped, and 13 mol O₂ burns 2 mol butane.
Key point: Kolbe: 2RCOO⁻ → R–R + 2CO₂ (anode), H₂ at cathode; CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ needs (3n + 1)/2 mol O₂.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting dipole moments, boiling and melting points of cis- and trans-1,2-dichloroethene, the structural condition for geometrical isomerism and methods of preparing alkenes
questions.question:
Data for the isomers of 1,2-dichloroethene are:
Isomer | Dipole moment (D) | Boiling point (K) | Melting point (K)
cis | 1.9 | 333 | 193
trans | 0 | 321 | 223
Which statement is correct?
options: A) The trans isomer is polar and therefore boils at the higher temperature; propene also shows geometrical isomerism
B) Both isomers have the same physical properties because they have the same formula; geometrical isomers can be interconverted by rotation about the double bond at room temperature
C) The cis isomer melts higher because it packs better in the crystal; alkenes can be prepared only by cracking

D) In the cis isomer the two C–Cl bond dipoles add up, so it is polar and has the higher boiling point (dipole–dipole attraction), while in the trans isomer they cancel; the more symmetrical trans isomer packs better in the crystal lattice and has the higher melting point; geometrical isomerism requires each doubly bonded carbon to carry two different groups (so propene and 1,1-dichloroethene show none); and alkenes can be prepared by dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides with alcoholic KOH, dehalogenation of vicinal dihalides with zinc, and acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) cis is polar (higher bp), trans packs better (higher mp); each sp² carbon needs two different groups; standard preparations as stated.
Concept: Restricted rotation about a carbon–carbon double bond allows geometrical isomerism: when the two identical atoms or groups lie on the same side of the double bond, the isomer is cis; on opposite sides, trans. Cis and trans isomers have different properties, such as melting and boiling points, dipole moment and solubility. Cis forms are generally more polar than trans forms; trans forms, being more symmetrical, fit better into the crystal lattice and have higher melting points.
Why: In the cis isomer the two polar C–Cl bonds point to the same side and their dipoles add to a resultant (1.9 D); in the trans isomer they are opposite and cancel (0 D), so the cis liquid has stronger intermolecular forces and boils higher. If one doubly bonded carbon carries two identical groups, the two possible arrangements are the same molecule. β-Elimination of HX from alkyl halides, removal of two halogens from vicinal dihalides with zinc, and dehydration of alcohols with concentrated H₂SO₄ are standard laboratory routes to alkenes.
Why not the others: (A) The trans isomer has zero dipole moment, and propene has two H atoms on C1. (B) The data show different properties, and the double bond prevents free rotation. (C) The trans isomer melts higher, and alkenes have several preparation methods.
Key point: cis: polar, higher bp; trans: non-polar, higher mp; each double-bond carbon needs two different groups.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Predicting electrode products for molten and aqueous NaCl and for CuSO4 with inert and copper electrodes, and calculating masses using Faraday's laws
questions.question: Which set of electrolysis results is correct, and what mass of copper is deposited by 2.0 A passed for 965 s through aqueous CuSO₄ with platinum electrodes? (Cu = 63.5, F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹)
options: A) Molten NaCl: H₂ at cathode; aqueous NaCl: Na at cathode; CuSO₄ with Pt: O₂ at cathode; 1.27 g Cu
B) Molten NaCl: Na at cathode, Cl₂ at anode; aqueous NaCl: Na at cathode, O₂ at anode; CuSO₄ with Cu electrodes: O₂ at anode; 0.318 g Cu

C) Molten NaCl: Na at cathode, Cl₂ at anode; aqueous NaCl: H₂ at cathode, Cl₂ at anode; CuSO₄ with Pt electrodes: Cu at cathode, O₂ at anode; CuSO₄ with Cu electrodes: Cu deposited at the cathode while the copper anode dissolves; 0.635 g Cu
D) Molten NaCl: Cl₂ at cathode; aqueous NaCl: H₂ at anode; CuSO₄ with Pt: Cu at anode; 0.0635 g Cu
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The products are as stated, and 0.635 g Cu is deposited.
Concept: Products of electrolysis depend on the nature of the material being electrolysed and the type of electrodes. With an inert electrode (Pt, Au), the competing reactions at each electrode are decided by their electrode potentials (and overpotentials); with a reactive electrode such as copper, the electrode itself can take part. Faraday's first law: the amount of chemical reaction at an electrode is proportional to the quantity of electricity passed; Q = It, and one mole of electrons carries 1 F = 96 500 C.
Given: I = 2.0 A; t = 965 s; Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.
Formula/Principle: Q = It; n(e⁻) = Q/F; n(Cu) = n(e⁻)/2.
Step 1: Q = 2.0 × 965 = 1930 C ⇒ n(e⁻) = 1930/96 500 = 0.020 mol.
Step 2: n(Cu) = 0.010 mol ⇒ m = 0.010 × 63.5 = 0.635 g.
Step 3: At the Pt anode, 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, so n(O₂) = 0.020/4 = 0.0050 mol.
Why: In molten NaCl only Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are present. In aqueous NaCl, water (E° = −0.83 V) is reduced in preference to Na⁺ (E° = −2.71 V), giving H₂; Cl₂ rather than O₂ forms at the anode because of the overpotential for oxygen. Cu²⁺ is easily reduced. A copper anode is oxidised to Cu²⁺ more easily than water, so it dissolves.
Why not the others: (A) Products are swapped, and the mass uses one electron per Cu. (B) Aqueous NaCl gives H₂, not Na, and the copper anode dissolves. (D) Electrodes are reversed, and the mass is off by ten.
Key point: Aqueous NaCl → H₂ + Cl₂; CuSO₄ (Pt) → Cu + O₂; Q = It, mass = (Q/F) × M/z.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Distinguishing order of reaction from molecularity, with pseudo-first-order reactions and the units of rate constants
questions.question: Which statement about the order and molecularity of reactions is correct?
options: A) Order is found experimentally and can be zero or fractional, while molecularity is the number of species colliding simultaneously in an elementary step and must be a whole number, rarely more than three; for a complex reaction the overall rate is decided by the slowest step, so order may differ from the stoichiometric coefficients; the acid hydrolysis of ethyl acetate in a large excess of water behaves as first order (pseudo first order) because the water concentration hardly changes; and the units of k are mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹, s⁻¹ and L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ for zero-, first- and second-order reactions
B) Order and molecularity are always equal and can both be fractional
C) Molecularity can be found only by experiment, while order is always the sum of the coefficients in the balanced equation
D) A pseudo-first-order reaction is one whose molecularity is zero
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Order is experimental (may be 0 or fractional); molecularity is a whole number for elementary steps; ester hydrolysis in excess water is pseudo first order; units as stated.
Concept: The rate law expresses the rate in terms of concentrations of reactants, each raised to a power that may or may not equal its stoichiometric coefficient; the sum of these powers is the order, which must be found experimentally. Molecularity is the number of reacting species (atoms, ions or molecules) taking part in an elementary reaction that must collide simultaneously; it is a theoretical concept and cannot be zero or fractional. For complex reactions the overall rate is controlled by the slowest step, the rate-determining step. Reactions that are not truly first order but behave as first order under given conditions are pseudo first order.
Why: In CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O → CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH (with H⁺), water is in such excess that its concentration stays almost constant, so rate = k′[ester]. The unit of k for an nth-order reaction is (mol L⁻¹)¹⁻ⁿ s⁻¹.
Why not the others: (B) Molecularity cannot be fractional, and order need not equal molecularity. (C) Order is found by experiment and need not equal the sum of coefficients. (D) Pseudo first order refers to observed order, not to zero molecularity.
Key point: Order: experimental, any value; molecularity: whole number, elementary steps only; pseudo first order when one reactant is in large excess.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Energy needed to convert a mass of gaseous zinc atoms to Zn2+ ions from ionisation enthalpies, with trends in ionisation enthalpy across and down the d-block
questions.question: The first and second ionisation enthalpies of zinc are 906 and 1733 kJ mol⁻¹. How much energy is needed to convert 1.00 g of gaseous zinc atoms into gaseous Zn²⁺ ions (Zn = 65.4), and which statement about ionisation enthalpies of transition elements is correct?
options: A) 13.9 kJ; ionisation enthalpies decrease sharply across each transition series

B) About 40.4 kJ; across a transition series ionisation enthalpies increase only gradually, because the electrons added go into the inner (n−1)d orbitals and shield the outer ns electrons from the increasing nuclear charge, and the 5d elements have higher first ionisation enthalpies than the 4d elements because of the poor shielding by the intervening 4f electrons (lanthanoid contraction), which helps make metals such as Pt and Au noble
C) 2639 kJ; ionisation enthalpies of 5d metals are lower than those of 4d metals because of their larger atoms
D) About 26.5 kJ; second ionisation enthalpy is always smaller than the first
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) About 40.4 kJ; gradual rise across a series and higher values for 5d metals because of poor 4f shielding.
Concept: Ionisation enthalpy is the energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom or ion. Across a transition series, nuclear charge increases with each element, but the added electrons enter the inner d orbitals, which shield the outer s electrons quite effectively, so ionisation enthalpies increase only gradually, much less than across a period of non-transition elements. In the third (5d) series, the filling of 4f orbitals before 5d results in poor shielding (lanthanoid contraction), so the 5d metals have relatively high ionisation enthalpies.
Given: IE₁ = 906 kJ mol⁻¹; IE₂ = 1733 kJ mol⁻¹; m = 1.00 g; M = 65.4 g mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: Energy = n × (IE₁ + IE₂).
Step 1: IE₁ + IE₂ = 906 + 1733 = 2639 kJ mol⁻¹.
Step 2: n = 1.00/65.4 = 0.0153 mol.
Step 3: Energy = 0.0153 × 2639 ≈ 40.4 kJ.
Why: Both electrons must be removed, so the two enthalpies are added; the second is larger because the electron is removed from a positive ion. The high ionisation enthalpies and high enthalpies of atomisation of the 5d metals explain their low reactivity.
Why not the others: (A) Uses only IE₁, and ionisation enthalpies rise across a series. (C) Gives the value per mole, and 5d metals have higher values. (D) Uses only IE₂ with an arithmetic slip, and IE₂ > IE₁.
Key point: Energy = n(IE₁ + IE₂); d-series IE rises gradually; 5d > 4d because of poor 4f shielding.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Linking spectrochemical strength to colour changes in nickel complexes, the colourlessness of anhydrous CuSO4 and the spin state of a d4 ion
questions.question: (i) Green [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ turns violet when excess ethane-1,2-diamine (en) is added, forming [Ni(en)₃]²⁺. (ii) Anhydrous CuSO₄ is white, while CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue. (iii) A d⁴ ion forms octahedral complexes. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) (i) en is a weaker-field ligand than water, so Δo decreases and the complex absorbs longer wavelengths; (ii) water molecules are coloured; (iii) a d⁴ ion always has four unpaired electrons

B) (i) en is a stronger-field ligand than water, so Δo increases and the complex absorbs light of shorter wavelength (higher energy), changing the complementary colour seen from green to violet; (ii) without water ligands there is no crystal field splitting in the visible range and so no d–d transition, so anhydrous CuSO₄ is white; (iii) if Δo < P (pairing energy) the configuration is t₂g³e_g¹ with four unpaired electrons (high spin), and if Δo > P it is t₂g⁴e_g⁰ with two unpaired electrons (low spin)
C) (i) The colour changes because nickel is oxidised to Ni³⁺; (ii) the copper ion in the hydrate has no d electrons; (iii) d⁴ complexes are always diamagnetic
D) (i) en and water give identical splitting; (ii) sulphate absorbs blue light only in the hydrate; (iii) the spin state of a d⁴ ion does not depend on the ligand
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Stronger-field en raises Δo; no ligand field → no d–d colour; d⁴ is high spin if Δo < P and low spin if Δo > P.
Concept: In crystal field theory, the ligands split the five degenerate d orbitals of the metal; in an octahedral field they split into a lower t₂g set and a higher e_g set separated by Δo. Ligands can be arranged in a spectrochemical series of increasing field strength: I⁻ < Br⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < S²⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < C₂O₄²⁻ < H₂O < NCS⁻ < edta⁴⁻ < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO. The colour of a complex is complementary to the light absorbed in the d–d transition. For d⁴, the fourth electron either enters e_g (if Δo < P, weak-field, high-spin) or pairs in t₂g (if Δo > P, strong-field, low-spin).
Why: (i) Replacing water by en increases Δo, so the absorption band moves to higher energy (shorter wavelength); the transmitted (observed) colour changes accordingly. (ii) In the absence of ligands, crystal field splitting does not occur, so the substance is colourless: removing water from CuSO₄·5H₂O destroys the blue colour. (iii) The choice depends on the balance between Δo and the pairing energy.
Why not the others: (A) en is stronger-field than water; water is colourless; d⁴ can be low spin. (C) Nickel remains +2, Cu²⁺ is d⁹, and d⁴ complexes have unpaired electrons. (D) The two ligands differ in field strength; the spin state depends on Δo versus P.
Key point: Stronger ligand → larger Δo → absorption at shorter λ; no ligands → no splitting → colourless; d⁴: Δo vs P decides spin.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Explaining, with reasons, how coordination compounds are used in gold extraction, chelation therapy, hardness estimation and medicine
questions.question: Which explanation of a use of coordination compounds is correct?
options: A) Gold dissolves in sodium cyanide solution without oxygen because gold is a very reactive metal
B) EDTA treats lead poisoning by precipitating lead as an insoluble salt that stays in the bones
C) Cis-platin is used for hardening water and has no medicinal use

D) Gold is leached from its ore by dilute NaCN in the presence of air, because Au forms the very stable complex [Au(CN)₂]⁻ (4Au + 8CN⁻ + 2H₂O + O₂ → 4[Au(CN)₂]⁻ + 4OH⁻), and is then recovered by displacement with zinc, which forms [Zn(CN)₄]²⁻; EDTA is used to treat lead poisoning because it forms a stable, soluble chelate with Pb²⁺ that is excreted; hardness of water is estimated by titration with Na₂EDTA because Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ form stable EDTA complexes; and cis-platin and related compounds effectively inhibit the growth of tumours
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Cyanide complex formation in gold extraction, chelation therapy with EDTA, EDTA titration for hardness, and cis-platin in cancer treatment.
Concept: Coordination compounds are of great importance in analytical chemistry, metallurgy, biology, industry and medicine. Hardness of water is estimated by simple titration with Na₂EDTA, since Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ form stable complexes with EDTA. Some important extraction processes of metals, such as those of silver and gold, make use of complex formation: gold combines with cyanide in the presence of oxygen and water to form the coordination entity [Au(CN)₂]⁻ in aqueous solution, and gold is separated by adding zinc. Excess copper and iron are removed by the chelating ligands D-penicillamine and desferrioxamine B, and EDTA is used in the treatment of lead poisoning. Cis-platin and related compounds inhibit the growth of tumours. Biologically important complexes include chlorophyll (Mg), haemoglobin (Fe) and vitamin B₁₂ (Co).
Why: The very high stability of [Au(CN)₂]⁻ lowers the effective electrode potential of gold so that oxygen can oxidise it; zinc, being more reactive, then reduces the complex back to gold. Chelating agents form multiple bonds to one metal ion, giving complexes that are stable and soluble enough to be removed from the body.
Why not the others: (A) Gold is noble; it dissolves only because the cyanide complex forms and oxygen acts as oxidant. (B) EDTA forms a soluble chelate that is excreted. (C) Cis-platin is an anticancer drug.
Key point: Stable complexes allow gold extraction (cyanide), detoxification (chelation), titration (EDTA) and cancer therapy (cis-platin).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ranking alkyl and benzylic halides for SN2 and SN1 reactivity from steric and carbocation arguments, with rate laws and stereochemical outcomes
questions.question: Which statement about SN1 and SN2 reactivity is correct?
options: A) For SN2, reactivity is CH₃Br > CH₃CH₂Br > (CH₃)₂CHBr > (CH₃)₃CBr, because the nucleophile attacks from the back side and bulky groups hinder it; for SN1, the order is reversed because the rate depends on the stability of the carbocation formed, and benzylic and allylic halides react very fast by SN1 because their carbocations are stabilised by resonance; doubling [nucleophile] doubles the SN2 rate (rate = k[RX][Nu⁻]) but does not change the SN1 rate (rate = k[RX]); SN2 gives inversion of configuration, while SN1 gives mainly racemisation
B) For SN2, tertiary halides react fastest because they form the most stable carbocations
C) Both SN1 and SN2 rates depend on the nucleophile's concentration to the same extent
D) SN1 gives complete inversion of configuration, and SN2 gives racemisation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) SN2: methyl > 1° > 2° > 3° (steric); SN1: reverse, fastest for benzylic/allylic; rate laws and stereochemistry as stated.
Concept: SN2 reactions follow second-order kinetics: the rate depends on the concentrations of both the alkyl halide and the nucleophile; the incoming nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group, through a transition state in which the C–Nu bond forms as the C–X bond breaks, causing inversion of configuration. SN1 reactions follow first-order kinetics: the rate depends only on the alkyl halide; the slow step is ionisation to a carbocation, which is then attacked by the nucleophile from either face, giving mostly racemisation.
Why: Bulky alkyl groups crowd the back side of the carbon and raise the energy of the SN2 transition state, so methyl halides react fastest and tertiary halides slowest. In SN1, the carbocation is stabilised by alkyl groups (inductive effect and hyperconjugation), so tertiary halides react fastest; allylic and benzylic carbocations are further stabilised by resonance.
Why not the others: (B) SN2 has no carbocation, and tertiary halides react slowest. (C) Only SN2 depends on [Nu⁻]. (D) The stereochemical outcomes are swapped.
Key point: SN2: back-side attack, steric control, inversion, second order; SN1: carbocation, stability control, racemisation, first order.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Identifying three isomeric C4H10O alcohols from the products of passing them over hot copper and from Tollens' and iodoform tests
questions.question:
Three isomeric alcohols X, Y and Z (C₄H₁₀O) are passed over heated copper at 573 K.
Alcohol | Product over Cu, 573 K | Further test on the product
X | aldehyde | silver mirror with Tollens' reagent; oxidation gives a straight-chain acid
Y | ketone | positive iodoform test
Z | alkene (2-methylpropene) | —
Which identification is correct?
options: A) X 2-methylpropan-2-ol; Y butan-1-ol; Z butan-2-ol
B) X butan-2-ol; Y 2-methylpropan-1-ol; Z butan-1-ol

C) X butan-1-ol (primary, dehydrogenated to butanal, which oxidises to butanoic acid); Y butan-2-ol (secondary, dehydrogenated to butanone, a methyl ketone that gives iodoform); Z 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary, which cannot be dehydrogenated and instead undergoes dehydration to 2-methylpropene)
D) X 2-methylpropan-1-ol; Y 2-methylpropan-2-ol; Z butan-2-ol
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) X butan-1-ol, Y butan-2-ol, Z 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
Concept: When the vapours of a primary or secondary alcohol are passed over heated copper at 573 K, dehydrogenation takes place and an aldehyde or a ketone is formed, while tertiary alcohols undergo dehydration to give alkenes. Aldehydes are oxidised by Tollens' reagent (silver mirror), and methyl ketones (CH₃CO–) give the iodoform test. Primary alcohols oxidise to aldehydes and then acids with the same carbon skeleton; secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones; tertiary alcohols resist oxidation under mild conditions.
Why: X gives an aldehyde, so it is primary; the acid is straight-chain, so X is butan-1-ol, not 2-methylpropan-1-ol (which would give the branched 2-methylpropanoic acid). Y gives a methyl ketone, so it is butan-2-ol (product CH₃COCH₂CH₃). Z cannot lose hydrogen from the carbinol carbon (no H on it) and instead loses water to give (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, so it is 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
Why not the others: (A) A tertiary alcohol cannot give an aldehyde. (B) Butan-2-ol gives a ketone, and 2-methylpropan-1-ol would give an aldehyde. (D) A tertiary alcohol cannot give a ketone, and butan-2-ol does not give 2-methylpropene.
Key point: Cu at 573 K: 1° → aldehyde, 2° → ketone, 3° → alkene.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: How the probability of disease given a positive test behaves as the prevalence p changes, using conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.question: A test detects a disease in 90 % of people who have it and gives a false positive in 10 % of people who do not. If the prevalence of the disease is \(p\), what is \(P(\text{disease}\mid\text{positive})\) as a function of \(p\), and how does it behave?
options: A) \(0.9\) for every \(p\), since the test is 90 % accurate
B) \(\dfrac{p}{1+p}\); it decreases as \(p\) increases
C) \(\dfrac{9p}{8p+1}\); it increases with \(p\), equals \(\tfrac1{12}\) at \(p=0.01\) and \(\tfrac12\) at \(p=0.1\), and tends to 1 as \(p\to1\)
D) \(\dfrac{9p}{10}\); it equals 0.09 at \(p=0.1\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(f(p)=\dfrac{9p}{8p+1}\), increasing, \(\tfrac1{12}\) at \(p=0.01\), \(\tfrac12\) at \(p=0.1\).
Given: \(P(+\mid D)=0.9,\ P(+\mid D')=0.1,\ P(D)=p\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(D\mid+)=\dfrac{P(+\mid D)P(D)}{P(+\mid D)P(D)+P(+\mid D')P(D')}\)
Step 1: \(P(D\mid+)=\dfrac{0.9p}{0.9p+0.1(1-p)}=\dfrac{0.9p}{0.8p+0.1}=\dfrac{9p}{8p+1}\)
Step 2: \(f'(p)=\dfrac{9(8p+1)-9p\cdot8}{(8p+1)^2}=\dfrac{9}{(8p+1)^2}>0\)
Step 3: \(f(0.01)=\dfrac{0.09}{1.08}=\dfrac1{12};\ f(0.1)=\dfrac{0.9}{1.8}=\dfrac12;\ f(1)=1\)
Worked derivation: \[p=0.01:\ \text{positives per 1000}=9\ (\text{true})+99\ (\text{false})\Rightarrow\tfrac{9}{108}=\tfrac1{12}\]
Check: \[f(0)=0\text{ and }f(1)=1\text{, as expected when nobody or everybody has the disease}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{for a rare disease most positives come from the large healthy group, so a positive result means little; as prevalence rises, true positives dominate}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{confuses }P(+\mid D)\text{ with }P(D\mid+)\); (B) \(\text{wrong formula and wrong behaviour}\); (D) \(\text{ignores false positives in the denominator}\).
Key point: \(P(D\mid+)\text{ depends strongly on prevalence; it increases with }p\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Domains, ranges and monotonicity of the graphs of sin⁻¹x and cos⁻¹x, their reflection property and their point of intersection
questions.question: Which statement about the graphs of \(y=\sin^{-1}x\) and \(y=\cos^{-1}x\) is correct?
options: A) Both have domain \([-1,1]\); \(\sin^{-1}x\) increases from \(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) to \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) and is the reflection of \(y=\sin x,\ x\in[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}]\) in the line \(y=x\); \(\cos^{-1}x\) decreases from \(\pi\) to 0; their sum is the constant \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\), and the graphs meet at \(\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\)
B) Both have range \([0,\pi]\) and meet at \((0,0)\)
C) \(\sin^{-1}x\) is decreasing and \(\cos^{-1}x\) is increasing; they meet at \((1,0)\)
D) Both have domain \(\mathbb R\); they never meet
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Domain \([-1,1]\); \(\sin^{-1}\) increasing, \(\cos^{-1}\) decreasing; sum \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\); intersection \(\left(\tfrac1{\sqrt2},\tfrac{\pi}4\right)\).
Given: \(y=\sin^{-1}x,\ y=\cos^{-1}x\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{graph of }f^{-1}=\text{reflection of graph of }f\text{ in }y=x;\ \sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Step 1: \(\sin^{-1}:[-1,1]\to[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}]\text{ (principal branch), increasing}\)
Step 2: \(\cos^{-1}:[-1,1]\to[0,\pi]\text{, decreasing}\)
Step 3: \(\sin^{-1}x=\cos^{-1}x\text{ and sum }\tfrac{\pi}{2}\Rightarrow\text{each}=\tfrac{\pi}{4}\Rightarrow x=\sin\tfrac{\pi}{4}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\)
Worked derivation: \[\cos^{-1}x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}-\sin^{-1}x\Rightarrow\text{the cos}^{-1}\text{ graph is the sin}^{-1}\text{ graph reflected in }y=\tfrac{\pi}{4}\]
Check: \[x=1:\ \sin^{-1}1=\tfrac{\pi}{2},\ \cos^{-1}1=0;\ \text{sum}=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{restricting sin and cos to intervals on which they are one-one gives inverse functions whose graphs are mirror images in }y=x\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{range of }\sin^{-1}\text{ is }[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}]\); (C) \(\text{monotonicity reversed}\); (D) \(\text{domain is }[-1,1]\).
Key point: \(\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\tfrac{\pi}{2};\ \text{graphs cross at }x=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Splitting a matrix depending on a parameter into symmetric and skew-symmetric parts and studying how their determinants vary
questions.question: For \(A(x)=\begin{pmatrix}x&2\\3&x\end{pmatrix}\), write \(A=P+Q\) with \(P\) symmetric and \(Q\) skew-symmetric. How do \(P\), \(Q\), \(\det P\) and \(\det Q\) depend on \(x\)?
options: A) \(P=\begin{pmatrix}x&2\\2&x\end{pmatrix},\ Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\); \(\det Q=-1\)

B) \(P=\begin{pmatrix}x&\tfrac52\\\tfrac52&x\end{pmatrix}\) and \(Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\tfrac12\\\tfrac12&0\end{pmatrix}\), so \(Q\) does not depend on \(x\); \(\det P=x^2-\tfrac{25}{4}\), which vanishes only at \(x=\pm\tfrac52\), and \(\det Q=\tfrac14\) for every \(x\)
C) \(P=\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\0&x\end{pmatrix},\ Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&2\\3&0\end{pmatrix}\); \(\det Q=-6\)
D) \(Q\) has diagonal entries \(x\); \(\det P=x^2-6\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(Q\) is constant; \(\det P=x^2-\tfrac{25}{4}\) (zero at \(\pm\tfrac52\)); \(\det Q=\tfrac14\).
Given: \(A=\begin{pmatrix}x&2\\3&x\end{pmatrix},\ A^T=\begin{pmatrix}x&3\\2&x\end{pmatrix}\)
Formula/Principle: \(P=\tfrac12(A+A^T)\ (\text{symmetric}),\ Q=\tfrac12(A-A^T)\ (\text{skew-symmetric})\)
Step 1: \(A+A^T=\begin{pmatrix}2x&5\\5&2x\end{pmatrix}\Rightarrow P=\begin{pmatrix}x&\tfrac52\\\tfrac52&x\end{pmatrix}\)
Step 2: \(A-A^T=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\Rightarrow Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\tfrac12\\\tfrac12&0\end{pmatrix}\)
Step 3: \(\det P=x^2-\tfrac{25}{4};\ \det Q=0-\left(-\tfrac12\right)\left(\tfrac12\right)=\tfrac14\)
Worked derivation: \[\det P=0\iff x=\pm\tfrac52;\ P+Q=\begin{pmatrix}x&2\\3&x\end{pmatrix}=A\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[P^T=P,\ Q^T=-Q,\ \text{diagonal of }Q\text{ is zero}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(x\text{ sits on the diagonal, which belongs wholly to the symmetric part; the off-diagonal difference }2-3\text{ alone forms the skew part}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(P+Q\ne A\text{ and that Q is not skew}\); (C) \(Q\text{ is not skew-symmetric}\); (D) \(\text{skew matrices have zero diagonal}\).
Key point: \(A=\tfrac12(A+A^T)+\tfrac12(A-A^T);\ \text{skew part has zero diagonal}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Second derivative of eˣ(sin x + cos x), the differential equation it satisfies, and counting zeros of y′ and y″ in [0, 2π]
questions.question: For \(y=e^x(\sin x+\cos x)\), which differential equation does \(y\) satisfy, and how many zeros do \(y'\) and \(y''\) have in \([0,2\pi]\)?
options: A) \(y''+y=0\); \(y'\) has 4 zeros and \(y''\) has none
B) \(y''-2y'+2y=0\); \(y'\) has no zeros and \(y''\) has 4
C) \(y''+2y'+2y=0\); each has 1 zero
D) \(y''-2y'+2y=0\); \(y'=2e^x\cos x\) has 2 zeros (\(\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\)) and \(y''=2e^x(\cos x-\sin x)\) has 2 zeros (\(\tfrac{\pi}{4},\tfrac{5\pi}{4}\))
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(y''-2y'+2y=0\); two zeros each for \(y'\) and \(y''\).
Given: \(y=e^x(\sin x+\cos x)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{product rule }(uv)'=u'v+uv'\)
Step 1: \(y'=e^x(\sin x+\cos x)+e^x(\cos x-\sin x)=2e^x\cos x\)
Step 2: \(y''=2e^x\cos x-2e^x\sin x=2e^x(\cos x-\sin x)\)
Step 3: \(y''-2y'+2y=2e^x(\cos x-\sin x)-4e^x\cos x+2e^x(\sin x+\cos x)=0\)
Worked derivation: \[y'=0\iff\cos x=0\Rightarrow x=\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{3\pi}{2};\quad y''=0\iff\tan x=1\Rightarrow x=\tfrac{\pi}{4},\tfrac{5\pi}{4}\]
Check: \[e^x>0\text{ never vanishes, so zeros come only from the trigonometric factors}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each differentiation multiplies by }e^x\text{ and shifts the trigonometric part; eliminating them gives a second-order equation}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(e^x\text{ factor rules out }y''+y=0\); (B) \(\text{miscounts the zeros}\); (C) \(\text{sign slip in the equation}\).
Key point: \(\text{zeros of }e^xg(x)\text{ are the zeros of }g\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Locating all local extrema of a quartic with three critical points by first and second derivative tests, and recognising it as a shifted square
questions.question: For \(f(x)=x^4-8x^3+22x^2-24x+1\), what are the local maxima and minima?
options: A) Local minimum at \(x=2\) (value \(-7\)); local maxima at \(x=1\) and \(x=3\) (value \(-8\))
B) Local minima at \(x=1\) and \(x=3\), both with value \(-8\) (the absolute minimum); local maximum at \(x=2\) with value \(-7\)
C) Only one local minimum, at \(x=2\)
D) Local minima at \(x=1\) and \(x=3\) with values \(-8\) and \(-10\); no local maximum
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Minima \(f(1)=f(3)=-8\); maximum \(f(2)=-7\).
Given: \(f(x)=x^4-8x^3+22x^2-24x+1\)
Formula/Principle: \(f'(c)=0;\ f''(c)>0\Rightarrow\text{min},\ f''(c)<0\Rightarrow\text{max}\)
Step 1: \(f'(x)=4x^3-24x^2+44x-24=4(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)\)
Step 2: \(f''(x)=12x^2-48x+44:\ f''(1)=8>0,\ f''(2)=-4<0,\ f''(3)=8>0\)
Step 3: \(f(1)=1-8+22-24+1=-8;\ f(2)=16-64+88-48+1=-7;\ f(3)=81-216+198-72+1=-8\)
Worked derivation: \[f(x)=(x^2-4x+3)^2-8=\left[(x-1)(x-3)\right]^2-8\ge-8\]
Check: \[\text{sign of }f':\ -\ (x<1),\ +\ (1<x<2),\ -\ (2<x<3),\ +\ (x>3)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the square form shows the minimum }-8\text{ is reached exactly where }(x-1)(x-3)=0\text{, and the hump between them peaks at the vertex }x=2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{max and min swapped}\); (C) \(\text{misses two critical points}\); (D) \(f(3)=-8\text{, and there is a local maximum}\).
Key point: \(\text{factor }f'\text{, test each root; spotting a perfect square confirms the result}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using odd and even parts of the integrand to evaluate a symmetric definite integral as a function of the limit a, and describing its behaviour
questions.question: Let \(g(a)=\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}\left(x^5+x\cos x+|x|\right)dx\) for \(a\ge0\). What is \(g(a)\), and how does it behave?
options: A) \(g(a)=0\) for all \(a\), since the integrand is odd
B) \(g(a)=\tfrac{a^6}{3}+a^2\); it grows like \(a^6\)
C) \(g(a)=2a^2\); it doubles when \(a\) doubles
D) \(g(a)=a^2\), because \(x^5\) and \(x\cos x\) are odd and integrate to zero over \([-a,a]\), while \(|x|\) is even; \(g\) increases for \(a>0\) and quadruples when \(a\) doubles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(g(a)=a^2\).
Given: \(g(a)=\int_{-a}^{a}(x^5+x\cos x+|x|)\,dx\)
Formula/Principle: \(\int_{-a}^{a}f=0\text{ if }f\text{ odd};\ \int_{-a}^{a}f=2\int_0^af\text{ if }f\text{ even}\)
Step 1: \(x^5\text{ and }x\cos x\text{ are odd}\Rightarrow\text{their integrals vanish}\)
Step 2: \(|x|\text{ is even}\Rightarrow\int_{-a}^{a}|x|\,dx=2\int_0^ax\,dx\)
Step 3: \(2\cdot\tfrac{a^2}{2}=a^2\)
Worked derivation: \[g(a)=a^2,\ g'(a)=2a>0\ (a>0);\ g(2a)=4a^2=4g(a)\]
Check: \[a=1:\ \int_{-1}^{1}|x|dx=\text{two triangles of area }\tfrac12=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{odd functions have equal and opposite areas on the two sides of 0; only the even part contributes}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(|x|\text{ is not odd}\); (B) \(x^5\text{ contributes zero over a symmetric interval}\); (C) \(\text{forgets the }\tfrac12\text{ in }\int x\,dx\).
Key point: \(\text{over }[-a,a]\text{, keep only the even part of the integrand}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding unknown upper limits from given values of definite integrals of a linear function and of ln x
questions.question: Find \(k>0\) such that \(\displaystyle\int_0^k(2x+1)\,dx=12\), and \(a>1\) such that \(\displaystyle\int_1^a\ln x\,dx=1\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(k=3,\ a=e\).
Given: \(\int_0^k(2x+1)dx=12;\ \int_1^a\ln x\,dx=1\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{FTC};\ \int\ln x\,dx=x\ln x-x\ (\text{by parts})\)
Step 1: \(\left[x^2+x\right]_0^k=k^2+k=12\Rightarrow(k+4)(k-3)=0\Rightarrow k=3\ (k>0)\)
Step 2: \(\left[x\ln x-x\right]_1^a=a\ln a-a-(0-1)=a\ln a-a+1\)
Step 3: \(a\ln a-a+1=1\Rightarrow a(\ln a-1)=0\Rightarrow a=e\ (a>1)\)
Worked derivation: \[\int_1^e\ln x\,dx=(e\cdot1-e)-(0-1)=1\]
Check: \[\int_0^3(2x+1)dx=9+3=12\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{evaluating the integral turns the condition into an equation for the limit; the sign condition picks the admissible root}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(k=4\text{ gives 20}\); (C) \(\int_1^2\ln x\,dx=2\ln2-1\ne1\); (D) \(k\text{ must be positive}\).
Key point: \(\int\ln x\,dx=x\ln x-x\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Behaviour of |a × b| + √3 a·b as the angle between two vectors varies, written as a single sinusoid with maximum, zero and minimum
questions.question: Vectors \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\) have \(|\vec a|=2\), \(|\vec b|=3\), and angle \(\theta\in[0,\pi]\) between them. Let \(f(\theta)=|\vec a\times\vec b|+\sqrt3\,\vec a\cdot\vec b\). What are the maximum and minimum of \(f\) and where is \(f=0\)?
options: A) Maximum 6 at \(\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\); minimum 0 at \(\theta=0\)
B) Maximum \(6\sqrt3\) at \(\theta=0\); never zero
C) \(f(\theta)=12\sin\left(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\): maximum 12 at \(\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6}\), zero at \(\theta=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\), minimum \(-6\sqrt3\) at \(\theta=\pi\)
D) Maximum 12 at \(\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{3}\); minimum \(-12\) at \(\theta=\tfrac{4\pi}{3}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(f=12\sin(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{3})\); max 12 at \(\tfrac{\pi}{6}\), zero at \(\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\), min \(-6\sqrt3\) at \(\pi\).
Given: \(|\vec a|=2,\ |\vec b|=3,\ \theta\in[0,\pi]\)
Formula/Principle: \(|\vec a\times\vec b|=|\vec a||\vec b|\sin\theta,\ \vec a\cdot\vec b=|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta;\ \sin\theta+\sqrt3\cos\theta=2\sin(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{3})\)
Step 1: \(f=6\sin\theta+6\sqrt3\cos\theta=12\sin\left(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\)
Step 2: \(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{3}\in\left[\tfrac{\pi}{3},\tfrac{4\pi}{3}\right]\)
Step 3: \(\text{max at }\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{3}=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\Rightarrow\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6};\ \text{zero at }\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{3}=\pi\Rightarrow\theta=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{min at the endpoint }\theta=\pi:\ 12\sin\tfrac{4\pi}{3}=-6\sqrt3\]
Check: \[|\vec a\times\vec b|^2+(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=36=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2\ \checkmark;\ f(0)=6\sqrt3,\ f(\tfrac{\pi}{6})=3+9=12\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\sin\theta\ge0\text{ on }[0,\pi]\text{ so }|\vec a\times\vec b|=6\sin\theta\text{; combining sine and cosine gives a single sinusoid}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores the dot-product term}\); (B) \(f(\tfrac{\pi}{6})=12>6\sqrt3\); (D) \(\tfrac{4\pi}{3}\text{ is outside }[0,\pi]\).
Key point: \(a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\sin(\theta+\alpha)\text{; respect the range of }\theta\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Direction cosines of a line through a point parallel to a vector, its Cartesian equation, and the distance of a point at a given parameter
questions.question: A line passes through \((1,2,3)\) parallel to \(2\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k\). What are its direction cosines and Cartesian equation, and what point corresponds to \(\lambda=3\) in \(\vec r=(\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k)+\lambda(2\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k)\), and how far is it from \((1,2,3)\)?
options: A) \(\left(\tfrac23,-\tfrac13,\tfrac23\right)\); \(\dfrac{x-1}{2}=\dfrac{y-2}{-1}=\dfrac{z-3}{2}\); \((7,-1,9)\), at distance 9
C) \(\left(\tfrac23,\tfrac13,\tfrac23\right)\); \(\dfrac{x-1}{2}=\dfrac{y-2}{1}=\dfrac{z-3}{2}\); \((7,5,9)\), at distance 9
D) \(\left(\tfrac13,-\tfrac23,\tfrac23\right)\); \(\dfrac{x-1}{1}=\dfrac{y-2}{-2}=\dfrac{z-3}{2}\); \((4,-4,9)\), at distance 9
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) DCs \(\left(\tfrac23,-\tfrac13,\tfrac23\right)\); \(\tfrac{x-1}{2}=\tfrac{y-2}{-1}=\tfrac{z-3}{2}\); \((7,-1,9)\), distance 9.
Given: \(\text{point }(1,2,3);\ \vec b=2\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k\)
Formula/Principle: \(l,m,n=\dfrac{a}{|\vec b|},\dfrac{b}{|\vec b|},\dfrac{c}{|\vec b|};\ \dfrac{x-x_1}{a}=\dfrac{y-y_1}{b}=\dfrac{z-z_1}{c}\)
Step 1: \(|\vec b|=\sqrt{4+1+4}=3\Rightarrow\left(\tfrac23,-\tfrac13,\tfrac23\right)\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{x-1}{2}=\dfrac{y-2}{-1}=\dfrac{z-3}{2}\)
Step 3: \(\lambda=3:\ (1+6,\ 2-3,\ 3+6)=(7,-1,9)\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{distance}=|\lambda||\vec b|=3\times3=9;\ \sqrt{36+9+36}=9\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[l^2+m^2+n^2=\tfrac{4+1+4}{9}=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{direction cosines are the components of the unit vector along the line; distance from the fixed point grows linearly with }|\lambda|\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{uses direction ratios as cosines and a wrong point in the equation}\); (C) \(\text{sign slip in the y-component}\); (D) \(\text{components interchanged}\).
Key point: \(\text{DCs}=\vec b/|\vec b|;\ \text{point at }\lambda\text{ is }|\lambda||\vec b|\text{ from the base point}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Maximising two objective functions over the same feasible region by corner points, including a case with infinitely many optimal solutions
questions.question: The feasible region is given by \(x+y\le4\), \(x+3y\le6\), \(x\ge0\), \(y\ge0\). What is the maximum of \(Z_1=3x+4y\), and what happens for \(Z_2=3x+9y\)?
options: B) \(Z_1\) max 12 at \((4,0)\); \(Z_2\) has no maximum

D) \(Z_1\) max 13 at \((3,1)\); \(Z_2\) max 18 at both \((3,1)\) and \((0,2)\), and hence at every point of the segment joining them, because the iso-profit lines of \(Z_2\) are parallel to the edge \(x+3y=6\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(Z_1\) max 13 at \((3,1)\); \(Z_2\) max 18 along the whole edge from \((3,1)\) to \((0,2)\).
Given: \(x+y\le4,\ x+3y\le6,\ x,y\ge0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{corner point method: the optimum of a linear objective on a bounded region occurs at a corner}\)
Step 1: \(\text{corners: }(0,0),(4,0),(3,1),(0,2)\ [x+y=4\text{ and }x+3y=6\Rightarrow y=1,x=3]\)
Step 2: \(Z_1:\ 0,\ 12,\ 13,\ 8\Rightarrow\max13\text{ at }(3,1)\)
Step 3: \(Z_2:\ 0,\ 12,\ 18,\ 18\Rightarrow\max18\text{ at }(3,1)\text{ and }(0,2)\)
Worked derivation: \[Z_2=3(x+3y)=3\times6=18\text{ at every point of the edge }x+3y=6,\ 0\le x\le3\]
Check: \[(0,4)\text{ violates }x+3y\le6\ (12>6)\Rightarrow\text{not feasible}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{if the objective's level lines are parallel to an edge of the region, all points of that edge give the same optimal value}\)
Why not the others: (A) \((0,4)\text{ is infeasible}\); (B) \(\text{the region is bounded, so a maximum exists, and }(3,1)\text{ gives more}\); (C) \(\text{misses the tie at }(3,1)\).
Key point: \(\text{two corners tie}\Rightarrow\text{every point of the joining edge is optimal}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Graph properties of aˣ and logₐx for a > 1 and 0 < a < 1, why a = 1 is excluded, and a value combining logs with reciprocal bases
questions.question: Which statement about \(y=a^x\) and \(y=\log_a x\) is correct, and what is \(\log_2 8+\log_{1/2}8\)?
options: A) Both pass through \((1,0)\); they are increasing for every \(a>0\); the value is 6
B) \(a^x\) is decreasing for \(a>1\); \(a=1\) gives the line \(y=x\); the value is \(-6\)

C) \(a^x\) passes through \((0,1)\) and \(\log_a x\) through \((1,0)\); their graphs are reflections of each other in \(y=x\); both increase if \(a>1\) and decrease if \(0<a<1\); \(a=1\) is excluded because \(1^x\) is constant (not one-one) so \(\log_1x\) is undefined; the value is 0
D) \(\log_a x\) is defined for all real \(x\); the value is 3
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Reflections in \(y=x\); monotonic by base; \(a\ne1\); value 0.
Given: \(a>0,\ a\ne1;\ \log_2 8,\ \log_{1/2}8\)
Formula/Principle: \(y=\log_a x\iff a^y=x;\ \log_{1/a}x=-\log_a x\)
Step 1: \(a^0=1\Rightarrow(0,1)\text{ on }y=a^x;\ \log_a1=0\Rightarrow(1,0)\text{ on }y=\log_ax\)
Step 2: \(\text{inverse functions}\Rightarrow\text{graphs symmetric about }y=x\)
Step 3: \(\log_28=3;\ \log_{1/2}8=\dfrac{\ln8}{\ln\frac12}=-3\)
Worked derivation: \[\log_28+\log_{1/2}8=3-3=0\]
Check: \[\left(\tfrac12\right)^{-3}=8\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(a^x\text{ is one-one only when }a\ne1\text{, which is needed for an inverse; the base decides increase or decrease}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(a^x\text{ passes through }(0,1)\text{ and decreases for }0<a<1\); (B) \(a^x\text{ increases for }a>1\text{; }1^x=1\); (D) \(\log_ax\text{ needs }x>0\).
Key point: \(a^x\text{ and }\log_ax\text{ are inverses (mirror images in }y=x)\text{; }\log_{1/a}x=-\log_ax\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Computing both compositions of a linear and a quadratic function, solving where they agree and finding the inverse of the linear one
questions.question: Let \(f(x)=2x+3\) and \(g(x)=x^2-1\). Find \((f\circ g)(x)\), \((g\circ f)(x)\), the values of \(x\) for which they are equal, and \(f^{-1}(x)\).
options: A) \(f\circ g=4x^2+12x+8,\ g\circ f=2x^2+1\); never equal; \(f^{-1}(x)=\tfrac{x+3}{2}\)
C) \(f\circ g=g\circ f=2x^2+1\) for all \(x\); \(f^{-1}(x)=\tfrac{1}{2x+3}\)
D) \(f\circ g=2x^2+2,\ g\circ f=4x^2+8\); equal at \(x=\pm\sqrt3\); \(f^{-1}(x)=x-3\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(2x^2+1\) and \(4x^2+12x+8\); equal at \(x=\tfrac{-6\pm\sqrt{22}}{2}\); \(f^{-1}(x)=\tfrac{x-3}{2}\).
Given: \(f(x)=2x+3,\ g(x)=x^2-1\)
Formula/Principle: \((f\circ g)(x)=f(g(x));\ f^{-1}:\ y=f(x)\Rightarrow x=f^{-1}(y)\)
Step 1: \(f(g(x))=2(x^2-1)+3=2x^2+1\)
Step 2: \(g(f(x))=(2x+3)^2-1=4x^2+12x+8\)
Step 3: \(2x^2+1=4x^2+12x+8\Rightarrow2x^2+12x+7=0\)
Worked derivation: \[x=\dfrac{-12\pm\sqrt{144-56}}{4}=\dfrac{-12\pm2\sqrt{22}}{4}=\dfrac{-6\pm\sqrt{22}}{2};\quad y=2x+3\Rightarrow f^{-1}(y)=\tfrac{y-3}{2}\]
Check: \[x=2:\ (f\circ g)(2)=9,\ (g\circ f)(2)=48\Rightarrow\text{composition is not commutative}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the order of composition matters: squaring after doubling-and-adding gives a different quadratic from doubling after squaring}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{compositions swapped and wrong inverse}\); (C) \(f\circ g\ne g\circ f\text{, and the inverse is not the reciprocal}\); (D) \(\text{algebra slips}\).
Key point: \(f\circ g\ne g\circ f\text{ in general; solve for }x\text{ to invert}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using the 2θ and 3θ identities with 5θ = 90° to find sin 18° exactly, then cos 36°
questions.question: Using \(\theta=18^\circ\), so that \(2\theta=90^\circ-3\theta\), find \(\sin18^\circ\) and \(\cos36^\circ\).
options: A) \(\sin18^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt5+1}{4},\ \cos36^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt5-1}{4}\)
B) \(\sin18^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt5-1}{4},\ \cos36^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt5+1}{4}\)
C) \(\sin18^\circ=\tfrac{1}{2},\ \cos36^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\)
D) \(\sin18^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt5-1}{2},\ \cos36^\circ=\tfrac{3-\sqrt5}{2}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\sin18^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt5-1}{4},\ \cos36^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt5+1}{4}\).
Given: \(\theta=18^\circ,\ 5\theta=90^\circ\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta;\ \cos3\theta=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta;\ \cos2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta\)
Step 1: \(\sin2\theta=\cos3\theta\Rightarrow2\sin\theta\cos\theta=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\)
Step 2: \(\cos\theta\ne0:\ 2\sin\theta=4(1-\sin^2\theta)-3\Rightarrow4s^2+2s-1=0\)
Step 3: \(s=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{4+16}}{8}=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt5}{4};\ s>0\Rightarrow s=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}{4}\)
Worked derivation: \[\cos36^\circ=1-2s^2=1-2\cdot\dfrac{6-2\sqrt5}{16}=\dfrac{8-6+2\sqrt5}{8}=\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{4}\]
Check: \[\tfrac{\sqrt5-1}{4}\approx0.309=\sin18^\circ;\ \tfrac{\sqrt5+1}{4}\approx0.809=\cos36^\circ\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the special angle with }5\theta=90^\circ\text{ links double and triple angles, producing a quadratic in }\sin\theta\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{swapped values}\); (C) \(\text{those are }30^\circ\text{ values}\); (D) \(\text{forgets the denominator 4}\).
Key point: \(\sin18^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt5-1}{4};\ \cos36^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt5+1}{4}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: For which n the statement 2ⁿ > n² holds, where the inductive step works, and the correct base case for induction
questions.question: For which natural numbers \(n\) is \(2^n>n^2\) true, and how is this proved by induction?
options: A) For all \(n\ge1\), with base case \(n=1\)
B) Only for odd \(n\)
C) For \(n\ge3\), with base case \(n=3\)

D) For \(n=1\) and all \(n\ge5\) (it fails at \(n=2,3,4\)); the inductive step \(2^{k+1}=2\cdot2^k>2k^2\ge(k+1)^2\) is valid whenever \(k^2-2k-1\ge0\), i.e. \(k\ge3\), so with base case \(n=5\ (32>25)\) the statement holds for all \(n\ge5\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) True for \(n=1\) and \(n\ge5\); induction from base case 5.
Given: \(P(n):\ 2^n>n^2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{PMI: }P(m)\text{ true and }P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1)\text{ for }k\ge m\Rightarrow P(n)\ \forall n\ge m\)
Step 1: \(n=1:2>1;\ n=2:4=4\ (\text{false});\ n=3:8<9;\ n=4:16=16\ (\text{false});\ n=5:32>25\)
Step 2: \(\text{assume }2^k>k^2;\ 2^{k+1}>2k^2\)
Step 3: \(2k^2\ge(k+1)^2\iff k^2-2k-1\ge0\iff k\ge1+\sqrt2\approx2.41\)
Worked derivation: \[k\ge5:\ 2^{k+1}>2k^2\ge(k+1)^2\Rightarrow P(k+1)\]
Check: \[n=6:\ 64>36;\ n=10:\ 1024>100\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the inductive step works from }k=3\text{, but the statement itself is false at 3 and 4, so the first true case after the failures, }n=5\text{, must be the base}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{fails at }n=2,3,4\); (B) \(n=3\text{ fails and }n=6\text{ works}\); (C) \(n=3\text{ is false, so it cannot be a base case}\).
Key point: \(\text{the base case must be true; the step alone proves nothing}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting integer values of k for which x² + kx + 4 = 0 has non-real roots, and the modulus and form of those roots
questions.question: For how many integers \(k\) does \(x^2+kx+4=0\) have non-real roots, and what can be said about these roots?
options: A) 9; the roots are real and equal
B) 8; the roots have modulus 4
C) 7 (\(k=-3,\dots,3\)); the roots are complex conjugates with product 4, so each has modulus 2; for example \(k=2\) gives \(-1\pm i\sqrt3\)
D) Infinitely many; the roots are purely imaginary
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Seven integers; conjugate roots of modulus 2.
Given: \(x^2+kx+4=0,\ k\in\mathbb Z\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{non-real roots}\iff D=k^2-16<0;\ \text{product of roots}=4\)
Step 1: \(k^2<16\iff-4<k<4\Rightarrow k\in\{-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\}:\ 7\text{ values}\)
Step 2: \(\text{real coefficients}\Rightarrow\text{roots }\alpha,\bar\alpha;\ \alpha\bar\alpha=|\alpha|^2=4\Rightarrow|\alpha|=2\)
Step 3: \(k=2:\ x=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{4-16}}{2}=-1\pm i\sqrt3\)
Worked derivation: \[|-1+i\sqrt3|=\sqrt{1+3}=2\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[k=\pm4:\ D=0\ (\text{equal real roots});\ \text{excluded}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a quadratic with real coefficients has complex roots in conjugate pairs, and their product equals the constant term}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{includes }k=\pm4\text{ and has the wrong nature}\); (B) \(|\alpha|^2=4\text{, not }|\alpha|=4\); (D) \(\text{finitely many; purely imaginary only for }k=0\).
Key point: \(D<0\Rightarrow\text{conjugate roots};\ |\alpha|^2=c/a\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving a system of three linear inequalities in one variable, writing the solution as an interval and counting its integers
questions.question: Solve the system \(2x-3<x+2\le3x+5\) and \(3(x-1)\ge2x-4\). What is the solution set, and how many integers does it contain?
options: A) \([-1,5)\); 6 integers
B) \((-1,5]\); 6 integers
C) \(\left[-\tfrac32,5\right)\); 7 integers
D) \([-1,5]\); 7 integers
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \([-1,5)\), containing 6 integers.
Given: \(2x-3<x+2;\ x+2\le3x+5;\ 3(x-1)\ge2x-4\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{solve each inequality, then intersect the solution sets}\)
Step 1: \(2x-3<x+2\Rightarrow x<5\)
Step 2: \(x+2\le3x+5\Rightarrow-3\le2x\Rightarrow x\ge-\tfrac32\)
Step 3: \(3x-3\ge2x-4\Rightarrow x\ge-1\)
Worked derivation: \[(-\infty,5)\cap\left[-\tfrac32,\infty\right)\cap[-1,\infty)=[-1,5)\Rightarrow\text{integers }-1,0,1,2,3,4\ (6)\]
Check: \[x=-1:\ -5<1\le2\text{ and }-6\ge-6\ \checkmark;\ x=5:\ 7<7\text{ false}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a system requires every inequality to hold, so the solution is the overlap; strict and non-strict signs decide the brackets}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{brackets reversed}\); (C) \(\text{ignores the third inequality}\); (D) \(x=5\text{ fails the strict inequality}\).
Key point: \(\text{intersect the individual solution sets; watch strict versus non-strict}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding an infinite G.P. from its sum and the sum of the squares of its terms, and how the sum of squares varies with r for a fixed sum
questions.question: An infinite G.P. has sum 4 and the sum of the squares of its terms is 48. What are its first term and common ratio, and how does the sum of squares behave as \(r\) varies in \((-1,1)\) with the sum fixed at 4?
options: A) \(a=6,\ r=-\tfrac12\); with the sum fixed at 4, the sum of squares is \(16\,\dfrac{1-r}{1+r}\), which decreases as \(r\) increases and takes every positive value
B) \(a=2,\ r=\tfrac12\); the sum of squares is constant
C) \(a=6,\ r=\tfrac12\); the sum of squares increases with \(r\)
D) \(a=8,\ r=-1\); the series converges
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(a=6,\ r=-\tfrac12\); sum of squares \(=16\tfrac{1-r}{1+r}\), decreasing in \(r\).
Given: \(\dfrac{a}{1-r}=4,\ \dfrac{a^2}{1-r^2}=48,\ |r|<1\)
Formula/Principle: \(S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r};\ \text{squares form a G.P. with first term }a^2\text{ and ratio }r^2\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{a^2}{1-r^2}=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\cdot\dfrac{a}{1+r}=4\cdot\dfrac{a}{1+r}=48\Rightarrow\dfrac{a}{1+r}=12\)
Step 2: \(a=4(1-r)=12(1+r)\Rightarrow16r=-8\Rightarrow r=-\tfrac12\)
Step 3: \(a=4\left(1+\tfrac12\right)=6\)
Worked derivation: \[a=4(1-r)\Rightarrow\dfrac{a^2}{1-r^2}=\dfrac{16(1-r)^2}{(1-r)(1+r)}=16\,\dfrac{1-r}{1+r}\to\infty\ (r\to-1),\ \to0\ (r\to1)\]
Check: \[6-3+\tfrac32-\dots=\dfrac{6}{3/2}=4;\ 36+9+\tfrac94+\dots=\dfrac{36}{3/4}=48\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{dividing the two sums eliminates }a\text{; the resulting ratio is a strictly decreasing function of }r\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{sum of squares }\tfrac{4}{3/4}\ne48\); (C) \(r=\tfrac12\text{ gives sum 12}\); (D) \(|r|=1\text{ does not converge}\).
Key point: \(\text{sum of squares of a G.P.}=\dfrac{a^2}{1-r^2}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: The fixed point of a family of lines, members parallel to the axes or through the origin, the member farthest from the origin, and the limiting member
questions.question: Consider the family \((2x+y-4)+\lambda(x-y+1)=0\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) The lines have no common point; \(\lambda=0\) gives the line through the origin
B) All lines pass through \((2,1)\); the member parallel to the \(x\)-axis has \(\lambda=2\)

C) All lines pass through \(P(1,2)\); \(\lambda=-2\) gives \(y=2\) (parallel to the \(x\)-axis), \(\lambda=1\) gives \(x=1\), \(\lambda=4\) gives \(y=2x\) (through the origin); the member farthest from the origin is perpendicular to \(OP\), namely \(x+2y=5\), at distance \(\sqrt5\); and the line \(x-y+1=0\) itself is reached only as the limiting case \(\lambda\to\infty\)
D) All lines pass through \((1,2)\), and every line through \((1,2)\) is obtained for some finite \(\lambda\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Fixed point \((1,2)\); special members as listed; farthest member \(x+2y=5\); \(x-y+1=0\) only as \(\lambda\to\infty\).
Given: \(L_1:2x+y-4=0,\ L_2:x-y+1=0;\ L_1+\lambda L_2=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(L_1+\lambda L_2=0\text{ passes through }L_1\cap L_2\)
Step 1: \(2x+y=4,\ x-y=-1\Rightarrow3x=3\Rightarrow P=(1,2)\)
Step 2: \((2+\lambda)x+(1-\lambda)y+(\lambda-4)=0:\ \lambda=-2\Rightarrow3y-6=0;\ \lambda=1\Rightarrow3x-3=0;\ \lambda=4\Rightarrow6x-3y=0\)
Step 3: \(\text{distance from O is largest when the line}\perp OP:\ \text{slope of }OP=2\Rightarrow\text{slope }-\tfrac12\text{ through }(1,2):\ x+2y=5\)
Worked derivation: \[d=\dfrac{|0+0-5|}{\sqrt{1+4}}=\sqrt5=|OP|;\quad \tfrac{2+\lambda}{1-\lambda}=\tfrac12\Rightarrow\lambda=-1:\ x+2y-5=0\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{dividing by }\lambda\text{: }\tfrac1\lambda L_1+L_2=0\to L_2\text{ as }\lambda\to\infty\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{any point on both }L_1\text{ and }L_2\text{ satisfies every member; the distance from O to a line through P cannot exceed }OP\text{, with equality for the perpendicular}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{they share }(1,2)\text{, and }\lambda=0\text{ gives }L_1\); (B) \((2,1)\text{ is not on }L_2\); (D) \(L_2\text{ is not obtained for finite }\lambda\).
Key point: \(L_1+\lambda L_2=0\text{ is the pencil through }L_1\cap L_2\text{ (except }L_2\text{ itself)}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Focus, directrix and latus rectum of the parabola x² = 20y, the ends of the latus rectum and the focal distance of a point
questions.question: For the parabola \(x^2=20y\), what are the focus, the directrix, the length of the latus rectum and its end points, and the distance of the point \((20,20)\) from the focus?
options: A) Focus \((5,0)\); directrix \(x=-5\); latus rectum 20; ends \((5,\pm10)\); distance 25
B) Focus \((0,20)\); directrix \(y=-20\); latus rectum 5; ends \((\pm2.5,20)\); distance 20
C) Focus \((0,-5)\); directrix \(y=5\); latus rectum 20; ends \((\pm10,-5)\); distance 15
D) Focus \((0,5)\); directrix \(y=-5\); latus rectum 20; ends \((\pm10,5)\); distance 25
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Focus \((0,5)\), directrix \(y=-5\), LR 20 with ends \((\pm10,5)\), focal distance 25.
Given: \(x^2=20y=4ay\Rightarrow a=5\)
Formula/Principle: \(x^2=4ay:\ \text{focus }(0,a),\ \text{directrix }y=-a,\ \text{LR}=4a,\ \text{ends }(\pm2a,a);\ \text{focal distance}=y+a\)
Step 1: \(a=5\Rightarrow\text{focus }(0,5),\ \text{directrix }y=-5\)
Step 2: \(\text{LR}=4a=20;\ \text{ends }(\pm10,5)\ [100=20\times5\ \checkmark]\)
Step 3: \((20,20):\ 400=20\times20\ \checkmark\text{ on the parabola}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{focal distance}=y+a=20+5=25;\ \sqrt{20^2+15^2}=25\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{distance to directrix}=20-(-5)=25=\text{distance to focus}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a parabola is the locus of points equidistant from the focus and directrix, so the focal distance equals the distance to the directrix}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{that is the parabola }y^2=20x\); (B) \(\text{uses }a=20\); (C) \(\text{opens downward instead of upward}\).
Key point: \(x^2=4ay:\ S(0,a),\ y=-a,\ \text{LR}=4a,\ SP=y+a\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding both values of the parameter k for which x²/25 + y²/k = 1 is an ellipse of eccentricity 3/5, with the major axis on either coordinate axis
questions.question: For which values of \(k>0\) does \(\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{y^2}{k}=1\) represent an ellipse of eccentricity \(\tfrac35\)?
options: A) Only \(k=16\)
B) \(k=16\) (major axis along the \(x\)-axis, foci \((\pm3,0)\)) and \(k=\tfrac{625}{16}\) (major axis along the \(y\)-axis, foci \((0,\pm\tfrac{15}{4})\))
D) \(k=25\), since then the ellipse is a circle
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(k=16\) or \(k=\tfrac{625}{16}\).
Given: \(\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{y^2}{k}=1,\ e=\tfrac35\)
Formula/Principle: \(e^2=1-\dfrac{b^2}{a^2}\text{ with }a^2\text{ the larger denominator}\)
Step 1: \(k<25:\ a^2=25,\ b^2=k\Rightarrow1-\tfrac{k}{25}=\tfrac{9}{25}\Rightarrow k=16\)
Step 2: \(k>25:\ a^2=k,\ b^2=25\Rightarrow1-\tfrac{25}{k}=\tfrac{9}{25}\Rightarrow\tfrac{25}{k}=\tfrac{16}{25}\Rightarrow k=\tfrac{625}{16}\)
Step 3: \(\text{foci: }c=ae:\ k=16\Rightarrow c=5\cdot\tfrac35=3;\ k=\tfrac{625}{16}\Rightarrow c=\tfrac{25}{4}\cdot\tfrac35=\tfrac{15}{4}\)
Worked derivation: \[k=\tfrac{625}{16}:\ c^2=a^2-b^2=\tfrac{625}{16}-25=\tfrac{225}{16}\Rightarrow c=\tfrac{15}{4}\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[k=16:\ c^2=25-16=9\Rightarrow c=3,\ e=\tfrac35\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the larger denominator decides which axis is major, so both orientations must be tested}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{misses the case }k>25\); (C) \(\text{uses }b^2=a^2e^2\); (D) \(k=25\text{ gives }e=0\).
Key point: \(\text{test both }k<25\text{ and }k>25\text{ when the major axis is not given}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Distance of closest approach of an alpha particle to a gold nucleus compared with the nuclear radius, and the energy needed to reach the nuclear surface
questions.question: A 4.0 MeV alpha particle is fired head-on at a gold nucleus (\(Z=79,\ A=197\)). Take \(\dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}=1.44\ \text{MeV fm}\) and \(R=R_0A^{1/3}\) with \(R_0=1.2\ \text{fm}\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) The closest approach is about 57 fm, while the gold nucleus has radius about 7.0 fm, so the alpha particle turns back long before touching the nucleus; it would need roughly 32 MeV to reach the nuclear surface
B) The closest approach is about 7 fm, so the alpha particle just touches the nucleus
C) The closest approach is about 28 fm; doubling the energy doubles it
D) The closest approach is about 114 fm; it does not depend on \(Z\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(r_0\approx57\ \text{fm}\gg R\approx7\ \text{fm}\); about 32 MeV needed to reach the surface.
Given: \(K=4.0\ \text{MeV},\ Z=79,\ z=2,\ ke^2=1.44\ \text{MeV fm},\ R_0=1.2\ \text{fm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{at closest approach }K=\dfrac{kZze^2}{r_0}\Rightarrow r_0=\dfrac{kZze^2}{K};\ R=R_0A^{1/3}\)
Step 1: \(r_0=\dfrac{1.44\times79\times2}{4.0}=\dfrac{227.5}{4.0}\approx56.9\ \text{fm}\)
Step 2: \(197^{1/3}\approx5.82\Rightarrow R\approx1.2\times5.82\approx7.0\ \text{fm}\)
Step 3: \(\text{energy to reach }R:\ K'=\dfrac{227.5}{7.0}\approx32.5\ \text{MeV}\)
Worked derivation: \[\dfrac{r_0}{R}=\dfrac{56.9}{7.0}\approx8\Rightarrow\text{pure Coulomb scattering; the nucleus is never touched}\]
Check: \[r_0\propto\dfrac{1}{K}:\ 4.0\times56.9\approx32.5\times7.0\approx227.5\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{all kinetic energy becomes Coulomb potential energy at the turning point; this distance only sets an upper limit on the nuclear size}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{confuses }r_0\text{ with }R\); (C) \(\text{wrong value, and }r_0\propto1/K\text{ halves when K doubles}\); (D) \(r_0\propto Z\).
Key point: \(r_0=kZze^2/K;\ \text{Rutherford-type scattering never reaches the nucleus at a few MeV for heavy targets}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Properties of the nuclear force (short range, saturation, charge independence, repulsive core) and the classification of nuclides as isotopes, isobars and isotones
questions.question: Which set of statements is entirely correct?
options: A) The nuclear force is long-range like gravity; \({}^{14}_{6}\text{C}\) and \({}^{14}_{7}\text{N}\) are isotopes
B) The nuclear force acts only between protons; \({}^{3}_{1}\text{H}\) and \({}^{4}_{2}\text{He}\) are isobars
C) The nuclear force is weaker than the Coulomb force between protons at 1 fm; \({}^{12}_{6}\text{C}\) and \({}^{13}_{6}\text{C}\) are isotones

D) The nuclear force is short-ranged (a few fm), nearly charge-independent (p–p, n–n and n–p alike), becomes strongly repulsive below about 0.5 fm and saturates; \({}^{14}_{6}\text{C}\) and \({}^{14}_{7}\text{N}\) are isobars, while \({}^{13}_{6}\text{C}\) and \({}^{14}_{7}\text{N}\) are isotones (7 neutrons each)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Short-range, charge-independent, repulsive core, saturating; isobars and isotones correctly identified.
Given: \(\text{isotopes: same Z; isobars: same A; isotones: same }N=A-Z\)
Formula/Principle: \(N=A-Z\)
Step 1: \({}^{14}\text{C},{}^{14}\text{N}:\ A=14\text{ for both}\Rightarrow\text{isobars}\)
Step 2: \({}^{13}_{6}\text{C}:N=7;\ {}^{14}_{7}\text{N}:N=7\Rightarrow\text{isotones}\)
Step 3: \({}^{12}_6\text{C},{}^{13}_6\text{C}:\ \text{same Z}\Rightarrow\text{isotopes, not isotones}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{saturation}\Rightarrow\text{binding energy}\propto A\ (\text{nearly constant }B/A\approx8\ \text{MeV})\text{ instead of }\propto A^2\]
Check: \[{}^{3}_1\text{H}(A=3)\text{ and }{}^{4}_2\text{He}(A=4)\text{ differ in A}\Rightarrow\text{not isobars}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the nuclear force binds all nucleons equally and only nearest neighbours, which explains the constant density and nearly constant B/A}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{force is short-range; C and N differ in Z}\); (B) \(\text{acts between all nucleons; A differs}\); (C) \(\text{nuclear force dominates at 1 fm; those are isotopes}\).
Key point: \(\text{same Z: isotopes; same A: isobars; same N: isotones}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Applying significant-figure rules to measured lengths, a computed volume, a sum and a quotient in a laboratory record
questions.question: A student records the radius of a sphere as 2.50 cm, adds two lengths 12.1 cm and 0.236 cm, and divides 4.80 g by 3.0 cm³. Which reported results follow the significant-figure rules?
options: A) Volume 65.44985 cm³; sum 12.336 cm; density 1.600 g/cm³
B) Volume 65 cm³; sum 12.34 cm; density 1.60 g/cm³
C) Volume 65.4 cm³; sum 12.3 cm; density 1.6 g/cm³
D) Volume 65.45 cm³; sum 12.3 cm; density 1.60 g/cm³
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 65.4 cm³, 12.3 cm, 1.6 g/cm³.
Given: \(r=2.50\ \text{cm (3 s.f.)};\ 12.1+0.236;\ 4.80\div3.0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{products/quotients: least number of s.f.; sums: least number of decimal places}\)
Step 1: \(V=\tfrac43\pi r^3=\tfrac43\pi(15.625)=65.45\ldots\Rightarrow65.4\ \text{cm}^3\ (3\text{ s.f.})\)
Step 2: \(12.1+0.236=12.336\Rightarrow12.3\ \text{cm}\ (1\text{ decimal place, set by }12.1)\)
Step 3: \(4.80/3.0=1.6\ (2\text{ s.f., set by }3.0)\)
Worked derivation: \[65.4498\to65.4\text{ (next digit 4 < 5, round down)}\]
Check: \[\tfrac43\text{ and }\pi\text{ are exact constants and do not limit the s.f.}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a result cannot be more precise than the least precise measurement that enters it}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{keeps calculator digits}\); (B) \(\text{over-rounds V and keeps too many digits elsewhere}\); (D) \(\text{V and density have too many s.f.}\).
Key point: \(\times,\div:\ \text{fewest s.f.};\ +,-:\ \text{fewest decimal places}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Conservation of angular momentum for a puck on a string pulled through a hole, and how speed, angular speed, kinetic energy and tension change
questions.question: A puck moves in a circle of radius \(r\) on a frictionless table, held by a string through a central hole. The string is pulled slowly until the radius is \(r/2\). By what factors do the speed, angular speed, kinetic energy and tension change?
options: A) Speed unchanged; angular speed ×2; KE unchanged; tension ×2
B) Speed ×2; angular speed ×4; KE ×4; tension ×8; the extra KE comes from the work done in pulling the string
C) Speed ×2; angular speed ×2; KE ×2; tension ×4
D) Speed ×\(\tfrac12\); angular speed unchanged; KE ×\(\tfrac14\); tension ×\(\tfrac18\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(v\times2,\ \omega\times4,\ K\times4,\ T\times8\).
Given: \(r\to r/2;\ \text{string force is central}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{central force}\Rightarrow\tau=0\Rightarrow L=mvr=\text{constant}\)
Step 1: \(mvr=mv'\tfrac r2\Rightarrow v'=2v\)
Step 2: \(\omega'=\dfrac{v'}{r/2}=\dfrac{4v}{r}=4\omega\)
Step 3: \(K'=\tfrac12m(2v)^2=4K;\ T'=\dfrac{m(2v)^2}{r/2}=8\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\)
Worked derivation: \[W_{\text{pull}}=K'-K=3K=\tfrac32mv^2>0\]
Check: \[L=I\omega:\ I'=m\tfrac{r^2}{4},\ \omega'=4\omega\Rightarrow I'\omega'=mr^2\omega\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the tension passes through the hole, so it exerts no torque about it; it does do work because the puck moves inward along it}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{assumes constant speed}\); (C) \(\omega=v/r\text{ gives a factor 4}\); (D) \(\text{reverses the effect}\).
Key point: \(L\text{ conserved under a central force; KE is not, when the radius changes}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Acceleration and string tension for a block on a smooth table connected to a hanging mass, compared with pulling the string by a force equal to that weight
questions.question: A 2.0 kg block on a smooth horizontal table is joined by a light string over a smooth pulley to a hanging 1.0 kg mass (\(g=9.8\ \text{m/s}^2\)). Then the hanging mass is removed and the string is pulled down with a constant force of 9.8 N. Compare the accelerations and tensions.
options: A) Both cases: \(a=4.9\ \text{m/s}^2,\ T=9.8\ \text{N}\)

B) Hanging mass: \(a=g/3\approx3.27\ \text{m/s}^2,\ T\approx6.53\ \text{N}\); pulling with 9.8 N: \(a=4.9\ \text{m/s}^2,\ T=9.8\ \text{N}\); the hanging mass also has to be accelerated, so its weight cannot all go into pulling the block
C) Hanging mass: \(a=g/2,\ T=9.8\ \text{N}\); pulling: \(a=g/3\)
D) Both cases: \(a=3.27\ \text{m/s}^2,\ T=6.53\ \text{N}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(3.27\ \text{m/s}^2,\ 6.53\ \text{N}\) versus \(4.9\ \text{m/s}^2,\ 9.8\ \text{N}\).
Given: \(M=2.0\ \text{kg},\ m=1.0\ \text{kg},\ F=9.8\ \text{N}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Newton's second law for each body; light string: same tension and same magnitude of acceleration}\)
Step 1: \(\text{block: }T=Ma;\ \text{hanger: }mg-T=ma\Rightarrow a=\dfrac{mg}{M+m}=\dfrac{9.8}{3}\approx3.27\ \text{m/s}^2\)
Step 2: \(T=Ma=2\times3.27\approx6.53\ \text{N}\)
Step 3: \(\text{pull: }T=F=9.8\ \text{N};\ a=\dfrac{9.8}{2.0}=4.9\ \text{m/s}^2\)
Worked derivation: \[T=\dfrac{Mm}{M+m}g=\dfrac{2}{3}\times9.8=6.53\ \text{N}<mg\]
Check: \[\text{hanger: }9.8-6.53=3.27=1.0\times3.27\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the falling mass accelerates, so the tension must be less than its weight; a fixed applied force has no inertia of its own}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores the hanging mass's inertia}\); (C) \(\text{wrong system mass}\); (D) \(\text{ignores the difference in the second case}\).
Key point: \(\text{tension in a moving Atwood-type system is less than the hanging weight}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Distinguishing conservative from non-conservative forces by path independence and closed-loop work, and relating potential energy, force and power
questions.question: Gravity, a spring force and kinetic friction act on bodies moved along different paths. Which set of statements about conservative forces, potential energy and power is correct?
options: A) Friction is conservative because it always acts; the work done by gravity depends on the path
B) A force is conservative if it is constant in magnitude; power is work multiplied by time

C) The work done by a conservative force (gravity, spring force) is independent of path and is zero round any closed path, so a potential energy with \(F=-\dfrac{dU}{dx}\) can be defined; friction is non-conservative because its work depends on the path length; instantaneous power is \(P=\vec F\cdot\vec v\)
D) Every force has a potential energy; the work done by friction round a closed path is zero
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Path independence, zero closed-loop work, \(F=-dU/dx\), friction non-conservative, \(P=\vec F\cdot\vec v\).
Given: \(\text{conservative}\iff\oint\vec F\cdot d\vec r=0\iff\text{work depends only on end points}\)
Formula/Principle: \(W_c=-\Delta U;\ F=-\dfrac{dU}{dx};\ P=\dfrac{dW}{dt}=\vec F\cdot\vec v\)
Step 1: \(\text{gravity: }W=-mg\Delta h\text{, set by end heights only}\)
Step 2: \(\text{friction: }W=-\mu mg\times(\text{path length})<0\text{ round any closed loop}\)
Step 3: \(\text{spring: }U=\tfrac12kx^2\Rightarrow F=-kx\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{block moved 2 m out and 2 m back with }\mu mg=5\ \text{N}:\ W_f=-5\times4=-20\ \text{J}\ne0\]
Check: \[P=Fv:\ 10\ \text{N at }3\ \text{m/s}\Rightarrow30\ \text{W}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{only forces whose work is path-independent store energy recoverably; friction turns mechanical energy into heat}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{friction is non-conservative; gravity's work is path-independent}\); (B) \(\text{constancy is not the test; power is work per unit time}\); (D) \(\text{non-conservative forces have no potential energy}\).
Key point: \(\oint\vec F\cdot d\vec r=0\text{ defines a conservative force}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.sub_topic: Position of the centre of mass of three point masses in a plane and the velocity of the centre of mass when two of them move
questions.question: Masses 1 kg at \((0,0)\), 2 kg at \((3,0)\) and 3 kg at \((0,4)\) (in metres) lie in a plane. Find the centre of mass. If the 1 kg mass then moves at 2 m/s along \(+x\) and the 2 kg mass at 1 m/s along \(+y\), with the 3 kg mass at rest, what is the velocity of the centre of mass?
options: C) \((2,1)\); \(v_{\text{cm}}=\left(\tfrac13,\tfrac13\right)\ \text{m/s}\)
D) \((1,2)\); \(v_{\text{cm}}=\left(\tfrac13,\tfrac13\right)\ \text{m/s}\), of magnitude \(\tfrac{\sqrt2}{3}\ \text{m/s}\) at \(45^\circ\) to the \(x\)-axis
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \((1,2)\); \(v_{\text{cm}}=\left(\tfrac13,\tfrac13\right)\ \text{m/s}\).
Given: \(m_1=1,\ m_2=2,\ m_3=3\ \text{kg};\ M=6\ \text{kg}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\vec r_{\text{cm}}=\dfrac{\sum m_i\vec r_i}{M};\ \vec v_{\text{cm}}=\dfrac{\sum m_i\vec v_i}{M}\)
Step 1: \(x_{\text{cm}}=\dfrac{0+6+0}{6}=1\ \text{m}\)
Step 2: \(y_{\text{cm}}=\dfrac{0+0+12}{6}=2\ \text{m}\)
Step 3: \(\vec v_{\text{cm}}=\dfrac{1(2,0)+2(0,1)+3(0,0)}{6}=\left(\tfrac26,\tfrac26\right)=\left(\tfrac13,\tfrac13\right)\)
Worked derivation: \[|\vec v_{\text{cm}}|=\sqrt{\tfrac19+\tfrac19}=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{3}\approx0.47\ \text{m/s},\ \text{direction }45^\circ\]
Check: \[\text{total momentum }(2,2)\ \text{kg m/s}=M\vec v_{\text{cm}}=6\left(\tfrac13,\tfrac13\right)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the centre of mass moves with the total momentum divided by the total mass}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{unweighted averages}\); (B) \(\text{divides by 2 instead of 6}\); (C) \(\text{coordinates interchanged}\).
Key point: \(M\vec v_{\text{cm}}=\vec p_{\text{total}}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Young's modulus, elastic energy density and stored energy from stress–strain data in the linear region, and the order of the characteristic points on the curve
questions.question: In the linear region of a wire's stress–strain curve, a stress of \(2.0\times10^8\ \text{Pa}\) produces a strain of \(1.0\times10^{-3}\). The wire has volume \(2.0\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}^3\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) \(Y=2.0\times10^{11}\ \text{Pa}\); energy density \(1.0\times10^5\ \text{J/m}^3\); stored energy 0.20 J; along the curve the proportional limit comes first, then the elastic limit and yield point, then the ultimate tensile strength, then fracture
B) \(Y=2.0\times10^{5}\ \text{Pa}\); energy density \(2.0\times10^5\ \text{J/m}^3\); stored energy 0.40 J
C) \(Y=2.0\times10^{11}\ \text{Pa}\); energy density \(2.0\times10^5\ \text{J/m}^3\); stored energy 0.40 J; the yield point comes before the proportional limit
D) \(Y=5.0\times10^{-12}\ \text{Pa}\); stored energy 0.10 J
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(Y=2.0\times10^{11}\ \text{Pa}\), \(u=1.0\times10^5\ \text{J/m}^3\), \(U=0.20\ \text{J}\).
Given: \(\sigma=2.0\times10^8\ \text{Pa},\ \varepsilon=1.0\times10^{-3},\ V=2.0\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}^3\)
Formula/Principle: \(Y=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon};\ u=\tfrac12\sigma\varepsilon;\ U=uV\)
Step 1: \(Y=\dfrac{2.0\times10^8}{1.0\times10^{-3}}=2.0\times10^{11}\ \text{Pa}\)
Step 2: \(u=\tfrac12(2.0\times10^8)(1.0\times10^{-3})=1.0\times10^5\ \text{J/m}^3\)
Step 3: \(U=1.0\times10^5\times2.0\times10^{-6}=0.20\ \text{J}\)
Worked derivation: \[u=\text{area of the triangle under the linear graph}=\tfrac12\sigma\varepsilon\]
Check: \[u=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{2Y}=\dfrac{4\times10^{16}}{4\times10^{11}}=1.0\times10^5\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the work done in stretching equals the area under the force–extension (or stress–strain) graph}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{multiplies instead of dividing and drops the }\tfrac12\); (C) \(\text{drops the }\tfrac12\text{ and wrong order of points}\); (D) \(\text{inverts Y}\).
Key point: \(u=\tfrac12\times\text{stress}\times\text{strain}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Applying the first law of thermodynamics with sign conventions to a general, an isothermal, an adiabatic and a cyclic process of an ideal gas
questions.question: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. What is \(\Delta U\)? Which of the following is also correct for an ideal gas?
options: A) \(\Delta U=300\ \text{J}\); in an isothermal process \(\Delta U=0\) so \(Q=W\); in an adiabatic expansion \(Q=0\) so \(\Delta U=-W\) and the gas cools; in a cyclic process \(\Delta U=0\) so the net heat absorbed equals the net work done
B) \(\Delta U=700\ \text{J}\); in an isothermal process \(Q=0\)
C) \(\Delta U=-300\ \text{J}\); in an adiabatic expansion the gas warms up
D) \(\Delta U=300\ \text{J}\); in a cyclic process the net work is always zero
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\Delta U=300\ \text{J}\), with the special cases stated correctly.
Given: \(Q=+500\ \text{J (absorbed)},\ W=+200\ \text{J (by the gas)}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta U=Q-W;\ \text{ideal gas: }U\text{ depends only on }T\)
Step 1: \(\Delta U=500-200=300\ \text{J}\)
Step 2: \(\text{isothermal: }\Delta T=0\Rightarrow\Delta U=0\Rightarrow Q=W\)
