Step 3: \(\text{adiabatic: }Q=0\Rightarrow\Delta U=-W;\ \text{expansion }(W>0)\Rightarrow\Delta U<0\Rightarrow T\downarrow\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{cycle: }\oint dU=0\Rightarrow Q_{\text{net}}=W_{\text{net}}=\text{area enclosed on the PV diagram}\]
Check: \[\text{energy: 500 J in = 200 J out as work + 300 J stored}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{internal energy is a state function, while Q and W depend on the path; the first law is energy conservation}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{adds W and confuses isothermal with adiabatic}\); (C) \(\text{sign errors}\); (D) \(\text{net work in a cycle equals the enclosed area, generally non-zero}\).
Key point: \(\Delta U=Q-W\text{ (W by the gas)}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Dependence of the mean free path of gas molecules on temperature, pressure, number density and molecular diameter, and why diffusion is slow
questions.question: The mean free path is \(\lambda=\dfrac{k_BT}{\sqrt2\pi d^2P}\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) Heating a gas in a sealed rigid container increases \(\lambda\) because \(T\) rises
B) Doubling the molecular diameter halves \(\lambda\)
C) \(\lambda\) is independent of pressure at constant temperature

D) Since \(\lambda=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\pi d^2n}\), heating in a sealed rigid container (fixed \(n\)) leaves \(\lambda\) unchanged; halving the pressure at constant \(T\) doubles \(\lambda\); doubling \(d\) makes \(\lambda\) one quarter; because \(\lambda\) is only of order \(10^{-7}\ \text{m}\) at NTP, molecules follow zig-zag paths and a smell spreads far more slowly than the molecular speed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\lambda\) depends on \(n\) and \(d\) only; unchanged at fixed \(n\); \(\lambda\propto1/P\) at fixed \(T\); \(\lambda\propto1/d^2\).
Given: \(\lambda=\dfrac{k_BT}{\sqrt2\pi d^2P}\)
Formula/Principle: \(P=nk_BT\Rightarrow\lambda=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\pi d^2n}\)
Step 1: \(\text{rigid sealed container: }n\text{ fixed; }T\uparrow\Rightarrow P\uparrow\text{ in proportion}\Rightarrow\lambda\text{ unchanged}\)
Step 2: \(T\text{ fixed, }P\to P/2\Rightarrow n\to n/2\Rightarrow\lambda\to2\lambda\)
Step 3: \(d\to2d\Rightarrow d^2\to4d^2\Rightarrow\lambda\to\lambda/4\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{NTP: }n\approx2.7\times10^{25}\ \text{m}^{-3},\ d\approx3\times10^{-10}\ \text{m}\Rightarrow\lambda\approx\dfrac{1}{1.41\times3.14\times9\times10^{-20}\times2.7\times10^{25}}\approx9\times10^{-8}\ \text{m}\]
Check: \[\text{units: }\dfrac{1}{\text{m}^2\cdot\text{m}^{-3}}=\text{m}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the mean free path is set by how crowded the molecules are and how big a target each presents, not by how fast they move}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{P rises with T at fixed n, cancelling}\); (B) \(\lambda\propto1/d^2\text{, so it becomes a quarter}\); (C) \(\lambda\propto1/P\text{ at fixed T}\).
Key point: \(\lambda=1/(\sqrt2\pi d^2n)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Phase relations among displacement, velocity and acceleration in SHM, and their values at the mean and extreme positions
questions.question: A particle executes SHM \(x=A\sin\omega t\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) Velocity and displacement are in phase; acceleration is maximum at the mean position
B) Acceleration leads displacement by \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\); speed is maximum at the extremes

C) Velocity leads displacement by \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) and acceleration is \(a=-\omega^2x\), i.e. \(\pi\) out of phase with displacement; at the mean position speed is maximum (\(A\omega\)) and acceleration is zero; at the extremes speed is zero and \(|a|=A\omega^2\); and \(v=\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2}\)
D) Velocity lags displacement by \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\); acceleration is in phase with displacement
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(v\) leads \(x\) by \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\); \(a=-\omega^2x\); extremes and mean values as stated.
Given: \(x=A\sin\omega t\)
Formula/Principle: \(v=\dfrac{dx}{dt},\ a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}\)
Step 1: \(v=A\omega\cos\omega t=A\omega\sin\left(\omega t+\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\Rightarrow\text{leads by }\tfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Step 2: \(a=-A\omega^2\sin\omega t=-\omega^2x\Rightarrow\text{phase difference }\pi\)
Step 3: \(v^2=A^2\omega^2(1-\sin^2\omega t)=\omega^2(A^2-x^2)\)
Worked derivation: \[x=0:\ |v|=A\omega,\ a=0;\quad x=\pm A:\ v=0,\ |a|=A\omega^2\]
Check: \[A=0.1\ \text{m},\ \omega=10\ \text{rad/s}:\ v_{\max}=1\ \text{m/s},\ a_{\max}=10\ \text{m/s}^2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each time derivative of a sinusoid advances its phase by }\tfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ and multiplies its amplitude by }\omega\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{v and x differ by }\tfrac{\pi}{2}\text{; a is zero at the mean}\); (B) \(\text{a leads x by }\pi\text{; speed is zero at the extremes}\); (D) \(\text{v leads; a is opposite to x}\).
Key point: \(x\to v\to a:\ \text{each leads the previous by }\tfrac{\pi}{2};\ a=-\omega^2x\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the dipole moment from the torque in a uniform field, the charge for a given separation, the work to rotate it through 180° and the net force on it
questions.question: An electric dipole of length 2.0 cm in a uniform field of \(3.0\times10^4\ \text{N/C}\) feels a torque of \(4.5\times10^{-4}\ \text{N m}\) when at \(30^\circ\) to the field. Which statement is correct?
options: A) \(p=1.5\times10^{-8}\ \text{C m}\); \(q=0.75\ \mu\text{C}\); work 0 to \(180^\circ\) is zero; net force \(qE\)

B) \(p=3.0\times10^{-8}\ \text{C m}\); \(q=1.5\ \mu\text{C}\); the work to rotate it from \(0^\circ\) to \(180^\circ\) is \(2pE=1.8\times10^{-3}\ \text{J}\); the net force is zero because the field is uniform
C) \(p=3.0\times10^{-8}\ \text{C m}\); \(q=1.5\ \mu\text{C}\); work \(pE=9.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{J}\); net force \(2qE\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(p=3.0\times10^{-8}\ \text{C m}\), \(q=1.5\ \mu\text{C}\), \(W=1.8\times10^{-3}\ \text{J}\), net force zero.
Given: \(2a=0.020\ \text{m},\ E=3.0\times10^4\ \text{N/C},\ \tau=4.5\times10^{-4}\ \text{N m},\ \theta=30^\circ\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tau=pE\sin\theta;\ p=q(2a);\ U=-pE\cos\theta\)
Step 1: \(p=\dfrac{4.5\times10^{-4}}{3.0\times10^4\times0.5}=3.0\times10^{-8}\ \text{C m}\)
Step 2: \(q=\dfrac{3.0\times10^{-8}}{0.020}=1.5\times10^{-6}\ \text{C}\)
Step 3: \(W=U(180^\circ)-U(0^\circ)=pE-(-pE)=2pE\)
Worked derivation: \[W=2\times3.0\times10^{-8}\times3.0\times10^4=1.8\times10^{-3}\ \text{J}\]
Check: \[\vec F_{\text{net}}=q\vec E+(-q)\vec E=0\text{ in a uniform field}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{in a uniform field the two forces cancel but form a couple, which rotates the dipole toward the field}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{forgets the }\sin30^\circ\text{ factor}\); (C) \(\text{work is }2pE\text{; net force is zero}\); (D) \(\text{uses }\cos30^\circ\).
Key point: \(\tau=pE\sin\theta;\ W_{0\to180^\circ}=2pE;\ F_{\text{net}}=0\text{ (uniform E)}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Charge distribution on a conductor with a cavity containing a point charge at the centre versus off-centre, and the field inside the conductor and outside it
questions.question: A neutral spherical conducting shell with a cavity has a point charge \(+q\) inside the cavity. Which statement is correct?
options: A) The inner surface carries no charge; the outer surface carries \(+2q\)
B) If \(+q\) is moved off-centre within the cavity, the field outside the shell changes direction

C) The inner surface carries \(-q\) and the outer surface \(+q\); the field inside the conducting material is zero; if \(+q\) is moved off-centre, the inner charge redistributes non-uniformly but the outer charge stays uniform, so the field outside (\(\tfrac{kq}{r^2}\), radial from the centre) does not change
D) The field outside the shell is zero because the conductor shields the charge
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Inner \(-q\), outer \(+q\) (uniform); the outside field is unaffected by the position of \(q\) inside.
Given: \(\text{electrostatic equilibrium}\Rightarrow E=0\text{ inside the conducting material}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Gauss's law: }\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=\dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}\)
Step 1: \(\text{Gaussian surface inside the metal: }E=0\Rightarrow q_{\text{enc}}=0\Rightarrow q_{\text{inner}}=-q\)
Step 2: \(\text{shell neutral}\Rightarrow q_{\text{outer}}=0-(-q)=+q\)
Step 3: \(\text{the metal screens the outer surface from the cavity, so the outer charge spreads uniformly over the sphere}\)
Worked derivation: \[r>R_{\text{outer}}:\ E\cdot4\pi r^2=\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\Rightarrow E=\dfrac{kq}{r^2}\]
Check: \[\text{total charge of the shell}=-q+q=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the inner charge arranges itself to cancel the cavity charge's field inside the metal; the outer charge feels only the conductor's spherical shape}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{violates Gauss's law inside the metal}\); (B) \(\text{the outer distribution stays uniform}\); (D) \(\text{shielding works from outside in, not inside out}\).
Key point: \(\text{a conductor screens its interior from the outside, but not the outside from a charge in its cavity}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Applying Kirchhoff's laws to two batteries in parallel feeding a load, finding branch currents, which battery is being charged and the power in the load
questions.question: Battery 1 (emf 10 V, internal resistance 2 Ω) and battery 2 (emf 4 V, internal resistance 2 Ω) are connected in parallel (positive to positive) across a 4 Ω resistor. Find the terminal voltage, the currents and the power in the 4 Ω resistor.
options: A) \(V=5.6\ \text{V}\); \(I_1=2.2\ \text{A}\) out of battery 1; \(I_2=0.8\ \text{A}\) into battery 2 (it is being charged); \(I_3=1.4\ \text{A}\) through 4 Ω; \(P=7.84\ \text{W}\)
C) \(V=5.6\ \text{V}\); both batteries supply current; \(I_3=3.0\ \text{A}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(V=5.6\ \text{V},\ I_1=2.2\ \text{A},\ I_2=-0.8\ \text{A},\ I_3=1.4\ \text{A},\ P=7.84\ \text{W}\).
Given: \(E_1=10\ \text{V},\ r_1=2\ \Omega;\ E_2=4\ \text{V},\ r_2=2\ \Omega;\ R=4\ \Omega\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{junction rule (KCL) at the top node with potential V: currents out of batteries}=\text{current into R}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{10-V}{2}+\dfrac{4-V}{2}=\dfrac{V}{4}\)
Step 2: \(7-V=\dfrac V4\Rightarrow\dfrac{5V}{4}=7\Rightarrow V=5.6\ \text{V}\)
Step 3: \(I_1=\dfrac{10-5.6}{2}=2.2\ \text{A};\ I_2=\dfrac{4-5.6}{2}=-0.8\ \text{A};\ I_3=\dfrac{5.6}{4}=1.4\ \text{A}\)
Worked derivation: \[P_R=I_3^2R=1.96\times4=7.84\ \text{W}\]
Check: \[I_1+I_2=2.2-0.8=1.4=I_3\ \checkmark;\ \text{loop: }10-2(2.2)=5.6\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the terminal voltage exceeds the 4 V emf, so current is pushed backwards through battery 2, charging it}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{averages the emfs without solving the circuit}\); (C) \(\text{wrong sign of }I_2\text{ and }I_3\); (D) \(\text{treats the batteries as in series}\).
Key point: \(\text{a negative branch current means the battery is being charged}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing magnetic fields at the centre of a circular loop, a semicircle and a long straight wire using Biot–Savart results, and the effect of rewinding a wire into two turns
questions.question: A current \(I\) flows in each case. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Field at the centre of a loop of radius \(R\) is \(\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi R}\); a semicircle gives half of that
B) A long straight wire at distance \(d\) gives \(\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2d}\); rewinding a loop into 2 turns doubles the field
C) The field at the centre of a loop depends only on the current, not on \(R\)

D) Centre of a loop: \(\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}\); centre of a semicircular arc: \(\dfrac{\mu_0I}{4R}\) (straight leads through the centre add nothing); long straight wire at distance \(d\): \(\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi d}\); if a wire forming one loop of radius \(R\) is rewound into 2 turns of radius \(\tfrac R2\), the field at the centre becomes 4 times larger
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\tfrac{\mu_0I}{2R},\ \tfrac{\mu_0I}{4R},\ \tfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi d}\); rewinding into 2 turns gives 4×.
Given: \(\text{loop radius }R;\ \text{wire length }2\pi R\text{ fixed}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Biot–Savart: }dB=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^2}\)
Step 1: \(\text{loop: every element at distance R, }\theta=90^\circ:\ B=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{4\pi R^2}(2\pi R)=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}\)
Step 2: \(\text{semicircle: length }\pi R\Rightarrow B=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{4R};\ \text{radial straight leads have }d\vec l\parallel\vec r\Rightarrow dB=0\)
Step 3: \(\text{2 turns of radius }\tfrac R2:\ B'=\dfrac{\mu_0(2)I}{2(R/2)}=\dfrac{2\mu_0I}{R}=4\times\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}\)
Worked derivation: \[\dfrac{B_{\text{loop}}}{B_{\text{wire}}}\Big|_{d=R}=\dfrac{\mu_0I/2R}{\mu_0I/2\pi R}=\pi\]
Check: \[I=1\ \text{A},\ R=0.1\ \text{m}:\ B=\dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}}{0.2}\approx6.3\ \mu\text{T}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{N turns multiply the field by N, and halving the radius doubles it again}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{that is the straight-wire formula}\); (B) \(\text{missing }\pi\text{, and the factor is 4 not 2}\); (C) \(B\propto1/R\).
Key point: \(B_{\text{centre}}=\dfrac{\mu_0NI}{2R};\ \text{same wire with N turns}\Rightarrow B\propto N^2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Using Curie's law to find the susceptibility of a paramagnet at a new temperature, and the temperature behaviour of diamagnetic and ferromagnetic materials
questions.question: A paramagnetic salt has susceptibility \(2.4\times10^{-5}\) at 300 K. Which statement is correct?
options: A) At 200 K its susceptibility is \(1.6\times10^{-5}\); a diamagnet has positive susceptibility that rises on cooling

B) At 200 K its susceptibility is \(3.6\times10^{-5}\) (Curie's law \(\chi\propto\tfrac1T\)); a diamagnet has small negative susceptibility that is almost independent of temperature; a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic above its Curie temperature
C) At 200 K its susceptibility is unchanged; ferromagnets become diamagnetic when heated
D) At 200 K its susceptibility is \(5.4\times10^{-5}\), since \(\chi\propto\tfrac{1}{T^2}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\chi(200\ \text{K})=3.6\times10^{-5}\); diamagnetic \(\chi<0\) and \(T\)-independent; ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic above \(T_C\).
Given: \(\chi_1=2.4\times10^{-5},\ T_1=300\ \text{K},\ T_2=200\ \text{K}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Curie's law: }\chi=\dfrac{C}{T}\Rightarrow\chi_1T_1=\chi_2T_2\)
Step 1: \(\chi_2=\chi_1\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}=2.4\times10^{-5}\times\dfrac{300}{200}\)
Step 2: \(\chi_2=3.6\times10^{-5}\)
Step 3: \(\text{ferromagnet above }T_C:\ \chi=\dfrac{C}{T-T_C}\ (\text{paramagnetic})\)
Worked derivation: \[C=\chi_1T_1=2.4\times10^{-5}\times300=7.2\times10^{-3}\ \text{K}\Rightarrow\chi_2=\dfrac{7.2\times10^{-3}}{200}=3.6\times10^{-5}\]
Check: \[\text{cooling increases }\chi\text{ for a paramagnet}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{thermal agitation opposes the alignment of permanent dipoles, so lower temperature means stronger alignment; diamagnetism comes from induced moments unaffected by temperature}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{inverts the ratio; diamagnet sign wrong}\); (C) \(\text{ignores Curie's law; heated ferromagnets become paramagnetic}\); (D) \(\text{wrong power of T}\).
Key point: \(\chi_{\text{para}}\propto1/T;\ \chi_{\text{dia}}<0,\ \text{T-independent}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Relations among field amplitudes, intensity and radiation pressure of an electromagnetic wave, and how intensity falls with distance from a point source
questions.question: An EM wave has electric field amplitude \(E_0\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) \(B_0=cE_0\); intensity is proportional to \(E_0\); radiation pressure on a reflector is \(I/c\)
B) \(E_0=B_0/c\); intensity from a point source falls as \(1/r\)
C) The electric and magnetic fields are parallel and oscillate out of phase

D) \(E_0=cB_0\); \(\vec E\), \(\vec B\) and the direction of travel are mutually perpendicular and \(\vec E\) and \(\vec B\) oscillate in phase; \(I=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0cE_0^2\propto E_0^2\), so from a point source \(I\propto\tfrac{1}{r^2}\) and \(E_0\propto\tfrac1r\); radiation pressure is \(I/c\) on a perfect absorber and \(2I/c\) on a perfect reflector
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(E_0=cB_0\); in-phase, mutually perpendicular; \(I\propto E_0^2\propto1/r^2\); pressure \(I/c\) or \(2I/c\).
Given: \(\text{plane EM wave in vacuum}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{E_0}{B_0}=c;\ I=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0cE_0^2;\ p=\dfrac{U}{c}\)
Step 1: \(\text{point source: }I=\dfrac{P}{4\pi r^2}\Rightarrow E_0\propto\sqrt I\propto\dfrac1r\)
Step 2: \(\text{absorber: momentum delivered per second per area}=\dfrac Ic\)
Step 3: \(\text{reflector: momentum reverses}\Rightarrow\dfrac{2I}{c}\)
Worked derivation: \[I=1000\ \text{W/m}^2:\ P_{\text{abs}}=\dfrac{1000}{3\times10^8}\approx3.3\times10^{-6}\ \text{Pa},\ P_{\text{ref}}\approx6.7\times10^{-6}\ \text{Pa}\]
Check: \[E_0=300\ \text{V/m}\Rightarrow B_0=\dfrac{300}{3\times10^8}=1\ \mu\text{T}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{EM waves carry energy and momentum; the momentum carried is the energy divided by c}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(B_0=E_0/c\text{, }I\propto E_0^2\text{, reflector }2I/c\); (B) \(\text{I falls as }1/r^2\); (C) \(\text{fields are perpendicular and in phase}\).
Key point: \(E_0=cB_0;\ I\propto E_0^2;\ p_{\text{rad}}=I/c\text{ or }2I/c\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Image formation by refraction at a single convex spherical glass surface with the object in air and then in water
questions.question: A convex spherical surface of radius 20 cm separates glass (\(n=1.5\)) from the medium containing an object placed 40 cm in front of the surface on the axis. Where is the image when the object is in air, and when it is in water (\(n=\tfrac43\))?
options: A) In air the refracted rays are parallel (image at infinity); in water the image is virtual, 60 cm in front of the surface on the object side
B) In air the image is real, 120 cm inside the glass; in water it is at infinity
C) In both cases the image is real, 60 cm inside the glass
D) In air the image is virtual, 40 cm from the surface; in water it is real, 60 cm inside the glass
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Air: image at infinity; water: virtual image 60 cm in front of the surface.
Given: \(n_2=1.5,\ R=+20\ \text{cm},\ u=-40\ \text{cm};\ n_1=1\text{ or }\tfrac43\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{n_2}{v}-\dfrac{n_1}{u}=\dfrac{n_2-n_1}{R}\)
Step 1: \(\text{air: }\dfrac{1.5}{v}+\dfrac{1}{40}=\dfrac{0.5}{20}=\dfrac{1}{40}\Rightarrow\dfrac{1.5}{v}=0\Rightarrow v=\infty\)
Step 2: \(\text{water: }\dfrac{1.5}{v}+\dfrac{4/3}{40}=\dfrac{1.5-4/3}{20}=\dfrac{1}{120}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{1.5}{v}=\dfrac{1}{120}-\dfrac{1}{30}=-\dfrac{3}{120}=-\dfrac{1}{40}\Rightarrow v=-60\ \text{cm}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{first focal length in air: }f_1=\dfrac{n_1R}{n_2-n_1}=\dfrac{20}{0.5}=40\ \text{cm}\Rightarrow\text{object at the focus}\]
Check: \[\text{water: }f_1=\dfrac{(4/3)(20)}{1/6}=160\ \text{cm}>40\ \text{cm}\Rightarrow\text{object inside focus}\Rightarrow\text{virtual image}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{surrounding the object with water reduces the index contrast, weakening the surface's converging power so the object falls inside the focal length}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{reverses the two cases}\); (C) \(\text{ignores the change of }n_1\); (D) \(\text{sign errors}\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{n_2}{v}-\dfrac{n_1}{u}=\dfrac{n_2-n_1}{R};\ \text{power depends on the index contrast}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Change in focal length of a glass lens when immersed in water and in liquids of equal and higher refractive index, using the lens maker's formula
questions.question: A thin glass lens (\(n=1.5\)) has focal length \(+20\ \text{cm}\) in air. What is its focal length in water (\(n=\tfrac43\)), in a liquid of index 1.5, and in a liquid of index 1.6?
options: A) 20 cm in all three, since the shape is unchanged
B) Water: \(+80\ \text{cm}\); index 1.5: infinite (it behaves like a plane glass plate); index 1.6: \(-160\ \text{cm}\), i.e. it becomes diverging
C) Water: \(+26.7\ \text{cm}\); index 1.5: \(+40\ \text{cm}\); index 1.6: \(+60\ \text{cm}\)
D) Water: \(+5\ \text{cm}\); index 1.5: zero; index 1.6: \(+160\ \text{cm}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(+80\ \text{cm}\), infinite, \(-160\ \text{cm}\).
Given: \(n_g=1.5,\ f_{\text{air}}=20\ \text{cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1f=\left(\dfrac{n_g}{n_m}-1\right)\left(\dfrac1{R_1}-\dfrac1{R_2}\right)\Rightarrow f\propto\dfrac{1}{(n_g/n_m)-1}\)
Step 1: \(\text{air: }(1.5-1)=0.5\)
Step 2: \(\text{water: }\dfrac{1.5}{4/3}-1=0.125\Rightarrow f=20\times\dfrac{0.5}{0.125}=80\ \text{cm}\)
Step 3: \(n_m=1.5:\ \dfrac{1.5}{1.5}-1=0\Rightarrow f=\infty\)
Worked derivation: \[n_m=1.6:\ \dfrac{1.5}{1.6}-1=-0.0625\Rightarrow f=20\times\dfrac{0.5}{-0.0625}=-160\ \text{cm}\]
Check: \[\text{a convex lens disappears optically in a liquid of the same index (no refraction at its surfaces)}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the lens bends light only because of the index difference at its surfaces; reversing the difference reverses the action}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores the medium}\); (C) \(\text{uses the wrong ratio}\); (D) \(\text{inverts the ratio and misses the sign change}\).
Key point: \(\text{relative index }n_g/n_m\text{ decides power; }n_m>n_g\Rightarrow\text{convex lens diverges}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Width of the central maximum and position of the first secondary maximum in single-slit diffraction, the effect of immersing the set-up in water, and energy reasoning for changing slit width
questions.question: Light of wavelength 600 nm falls on a slit of width 0.20 mm and the pattern is seen on a screen 1.5 m away. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Central maximum width 4.5 mm; first secondary maximum at 9.0 mm; in water the width increases
B) Central maximum width 9.0 mm; the central width doubles if the slit width doubles

C) Central maximum width 9.0 mm; first secondary maximum about 6.75 mm from the centre; in water (\(n=\tfrac43\)) the width becomes 6.75 mm; doubling the slit width halves the central width, lets through twice the light and makes the central peak intensity about 4 times larger
D) Central maximum width 18 mm; it does not depend on the medium
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 9.0 mm; secondary maximum ≈ 6.75 mm; 6.75 mm in water; doubling the width gives 4× peak intensity.
Given: \(\lambda=600\ \text{nm},\ a=0.20\ \text{mm},\ D=1.5\ \text{m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{minima: }a\sin\theta=m\lambda;\ \text{central width}=\dfrac{2\lambda D}{a};\ \text{first secondary maximum near }a\sin\theta=\tfrac32\lambda\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{2\lambda D}{a}=\dfrac{2\times600\times10^{-9}\times1.5}{2.0\times10^{-4}}=9.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}=9.0\ \text{mm}\)
Step 2: \(y_1'=\dfrac{1.5\lambda D}{a}=\dfrac34\times9.0=6.75\ \text{mm}\)
Step 3: \(\text{water: }\lambda'=\dfrac{\lambda}{n}=450\ \text{nm}\Rightarrow\text{width}=\dfrac{9.0}{4/3}=6.75\ \text{mm}\)
Worked derivation: \[a\to2a:\ \text{power through slit}\times2,\ \text{central width}\times\tfrac12\Rightarrow\text{peak intensity}\times4\ (I_0\propto a^2)\]
Check: \[\theta_1=\dfrac{\lambda}{a}=3\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad (small)}\Rightarrow\text{small-angle approximation valid}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{diffraction spreading is set by }\lambda/a\text{; shorter wavelength in water or a wider slit both narrow the pattern}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{half-width given as width; water narrows the pattern}\); (B) \(\text{width}\propto1/a\); (D) \(\text{doubles the width again; depends on the medium through }\lambda\).
Key point: \(\text{central width}=2\lambda D/a;\ I_0\propto a^2\)
